title: Data Field Theory: Theory and Applications of the Functional Renormalization Group for Signal Detection
summary: We review the renormalization group framework for signal detection in high-dimensional data, tailored to the regime where the signal may be of extensive rank and does not separate from the noise bulk as isolated spikes. The framework provides a conceptually simple criterion for distinguishing signal from noise within a quasi-continuous spectral region near a random-matrix universality class. This scenario lies beyond the reach of standard methods such as the Baik-Ben Arous-Péché threshold, which requires eigenvalues to be cleanly separated from the bulk. The renormalization group approach, by contrast, directly tracks spectral deformations and consistently yields a lower limit of detection without relying on spike separation. We review results that identify the presence of a signal by testing the stability of the Gaussian fixed point of an effective field theory for the collective behaviour of the degrees of freedom in the spectral tail, where the signal resides. We also discuss how the scale dependence of the canonical dimension, induced by the signal, manifests as a dimensional phase transition.

AI.tldr: This paper reviews a renormalization group (RG) framework for signal detection in high-dimensional data when the signal has extensive rank and overlaps with the noise bulk, moving beyond the standard Baik-Ben Arous-Péché threshold. The RG approach tracks spectral deformations near random-matrix universality classes, detects signals via stability tests of the Gaussian fixed point in an effective field theory, and reveals signal-induced dimensional phase transitions.
AI.motivation: Standard signal detection methods (e.g., the BBP threshold) require eigenvalues to be cleanly separated from the noise bulk. However, in high-dimensional settings where the signal has extensive rank and does not form isolated spikes, these methods fail. A new conceptual framework is needed to detect signals that reside within quasi-continuous spectral regions near random-matrix universality classes.
AI.method: The paper employs a renormalization group framework based on an effective field theory describing the collective behaviour of degrees of freedom in the spectral tail. Signal detection is recast as testing the stability of the Gaussian fixed point of this field theory. The framework tracks spectral deformations directly and analyzes the scale dependence of the canonical dimension induced by the signal, which manifests as a dimensional phase transition.
AI.result: The RG approach consistently yields a lower limit of detection without relying on spike separation, providing a conceptually simple criterion for distinguishing signal from noise in the quasi-continuous spectral regime. The framework successfully identifies signals beyond the reach of standard BBP-based methods and reveals dimensional phase transitions driven by the signal.
AI.conclusion: The renormalization group framework offers a principled and generalizable alternative to standard threshold-based signal detection methods, extending signal detection capability to regimes where signals overlap with the noise bulk and exhibit extensive rank.

title: Unveiling Amplitude Distributions via the Ordinal Language of Random Walks
summary: Ordinal patterns are widely used to characterize temporal organization in time series, yet they are often considered insensitive to the amplitude distribution of the data. In this work, we show that this limitation can be overcome by considering the ordinal structure of integrated time series. We investigate random walks generated from independent non-Gaussian increments and derive analytical expressions for the ordinal pattern probabilities associated with them. We show that for symmetric distributions, the probabilities of some ordinal patterns are fully determined by symmetry arguments, while those for the remaining patterns depend explicitly on the shape of the increments distribution. Numerical simulations based on $q$-Gaussian increments validate the theoretical predictions. We further show that the construction of the random walk itself plays a fundamental role in the accurate characterization of non-Gaussian fluctuations, as different centering procedures may significantly affect the resulting ordinal statistics. Finally, we validate the proposed framework using financial time series, showing that the ordinal distributions of integrated logarithmic returns capture non-Gaussian features consistent with a cubic law.

AI.tldr: This paper overcomes the perceived insensitivity of ordinal pattern analysis to amplitude distributions by analyzing ordinal patterns of integrated (random walk) time series derived from independent non-Gaussian increments. Analytical expressions for ordinal pattern probabilities are derived, validated with q-Gaussian simulations, and applied to financial data revealing cubic-law non-Gaussian features.
AI.motivation: Ordinal patterns are a popular tool for characterizing temporal organization in time series, but they are generally considered insensitive to the amplitude distribution of the data. The authors aim to overcome this limitation by leveraging the ordinal structure of integrated time series (random walks), thereby enabling ordinal analysis to capture non-Gaussian features of data.
AI.method: The authors derive analytical expressions for ordinal pattern probabilities of random walks generated from independent non-Gaussian increments. They use symmetry arguments for symmetric distributions to determine some pattern probabilities exactly, while remaining patterns depend on the increment distribution's shape. They validate predictions via numerical simulations with q-Gaussian increments and apply the framework to financial log-return time series.
AI.result: For symmetric distributions, some ordinal pattern probabilities are fully fixed by symmetry, while others explicitly depend on the distribution shape. Numerical simulations with q-Gaussian increments confirm theoretical predictions. The centering procedure used to construct the random walk significantly impacts ordinal statistics. Applications to financial time series show that ordinal distributions of integrated logarithmic returns capture non-Gaussian features consistent with a cubic law.
AI.conclusion: The ordinal structure of integrated time series provides a viable and sensitive approach to characterize amplitude (non-Gaussian) features of data, overcoming the classical limitation of ordinal pattern analysis. The framework is validated analytically, numerically, and empirically on financial data.

title: Optical Dipole Trap for Hg Atoms
summary: We report the first realization of an optical dipole trap (ODT) for ultracold mercury atoms, overcoming the challenge posed by the exceptionally low polarizability of Hg and the resulting weak optical trapping potential. We demonstrate the transfer of six naturally abundant Hg isotopes from a magneto-optical trap (MOT) into the ODT and characterize its loading dynamics, trap depth, and lifetime. Confinement of dense samples of ultracold Hg opens new opportunities for studies of isotope-dependent collisions and photoassociation and provides a route toward quantum degeneracy.

AI.tldr: The authors report the first-ever realization of an optical dipole trap (ODT) for ultracold mercury atoms, overcoming the challenge of Hg's exceptionally low polarizability. They successfully transfer all six naturally abundant Hg isotopes from a magneto-optical trap into the ODT and characterize its loading dynamics, trap depth, and lifetime, enabling studies of isotope-dependent collisions, photoassociation, and a path toward quantum degeneracy.
AI.motivation: Ultracold mercury atoms are of interest for studies of isotope-dependent collisions, photoassociation, and quantum degenerate gases, but their exceptionally low polarizability results in weak optical trapping potentials, making ODT realization challenging. This work aims to overcome this challenge and achieve the first ODT for ultracold Hg.
AI.method: The authors realize an optical dipole trap for ultracold mercury atoms by addressing the low polarizability challenge. They demonstrate loading of all six naturally abundant Hg isotopes from a magneto-optical trap into the ODT and characterize the trap through loading dynamics, trap depth measurements, and lifetime studies.
AI.result: Successful confinement of dense samples of ultracold Hg atoms in an optical dipole trap is achieved, with the transfer of all six naturally abundant Hg isotopes demonstrated and the trap's loading dynamics, depth, and lifetime characterized.
AI.conclusion: The realization of the first ODT for ultracold mercury opens new opportunities for studying isotope-dependent collisions and photoassociation, and provides a viable route toward achieving quantum degeneracy with Hg atoms.

title: Phase noise analysis and control of VO$_2$-based relaxation type oscillators
summary: VO$_2$-based relaxation oscillators form a rapidly developing field that finds applications in neuromorphic computing, Ising machines, and numerous signal processing concepts. These oscillators operate in a deeply nonlinear relaxation regime based on rapid phase transitions between insulating and metallic states in the VO$_2$ material. This process is governed by thermal effects, which lead to additional voltage fluctuations and contribute to a considerably wide spectral linewidth in the VO$_2$-based oscillator signal. In this work, we thoroughly study the phase noise in VO$_2$-based relaxation oscillators and demonstrate that the broadening of the generation spectrum linewidth at low oscillation frequencies is caused by an increased susceptibility to thermal fluctuations during the incubation phase. We explore the types of noise affecting oscillator stability and show that synchronization with an external square-wave signal improves the phase noise more effectively than a sinusoidal-shape injection locking signal.

AI.tldr: This paper studies phase noise in VO₂-based relaxation oscillators, showing that the spectral linewidth broadening at low frequencies is caused by increased susceptibility to thermal fluctuations during the incubation phase, and demonstrates that square-wave synchronization improves phase noise more effectively than sinusoidal injection locking.
AI.motivation: VO₂-based relaxation oscillators are promising for neuromorphic computing and Ising machines, but they suffer from wide spectral linewidths due to thermal effects. Understanding and mitigating phase noise is critical for improving oscillator stability and performance in practical applications.
AI.method: The authors thoroughly analyze phase noise in VO₂-based relaxation oscillators, identifying noise types affecting oscillator stability, and experimentally compare phase noise improvement between synchronization with an external square-wave signal versus sinusoidal-shape injection locking.
AI.result: The study demonstrates that linewidth broadening at low oscillation frequencies stems from increased susceptibility to thermal fluctuations during the incubation phase, and that square-wave synchronization yields better phase noise improvement than sinusoidal injection locking.
AI.conclusion: The phase noise of VO₂-based oscillators is dominated by thermal fluctuations during the incubation phase, and external synchronization with square-wave signals provides a more effective noise suppression strategy than sinusoidal injection locking for improving oscillator stability.

title: Anomalous Microwave Response in YBCO Resonators beyond the Two-Level-System Model
summary: We report the microwave response of coplanar-waveguide (CPW) resonators fabricated from $\mathrm{YBa_2Cu_3O_{7-δ}}$ (YBCO) thin films over temperatures from approximately $70~\mathrm{mK}$ to $40~\mathrm{K}$. The resonators exhibit internal quality factors $Q_\mathrm{i}$ in the range of $4\times10^3$ to $10^4$ at 70 mK, which increase to a maximum of approximately $8\times10^3$ to $1.2\times10^4$ near $6~\mathrm{K}$. At low temperatures, both $Q_\mathrm{i}$ and the fractional shift of the resonance frequency $Δf_\mathrm{r}/f_\mathrm{r}$ increases with temperature, qualitatively resembling behavior commonly associated with two-level-system (TLS) defects. However, neither response saturates on the temperature scale set by the resonator frequency, and the loss exhibits no observable microwave-power dependence. We show that low-temperature frequency upturn may be better described by an additional paramagnetic response associated with defect-induced local moments or Andreev bound states, while the low-temperature loss follows an approximately logarithmic temperature dependence whose microscopic origin remains unresolved. These measurements establish the millikelvin performance of patterned YBCO resonators and show that their low-temperature response cannot be understood within the conventional TLS framework alone.

AI.tldr: The paper reports microwave measurements of YBCO coplanar-waveguide resonators from ~70 mK to 40 K. Q_i ranges from 4×10^3 to 10^4 at 70 mK, peaking near 6 K. Low-temperature responses resemble TLS behavior but lack saturation and power dependence. The low-temperature frequency upturn is better explained by paramagnetic defect moments or Andreev bound states, while the loss follows a logarithmic temperature dependence of unresolved origin, indicating YBCO resonators cannot be described by the conventional TLS framework alone.
AI.motivation: To establish the millikelvin performance of patterned YBCO resonators and determine whether their low-temperature microwave response can be understood within the conventional two-level-system (TLS) framework, given growing interest in high-temperature superconducting resonators for quantum applications.
AI.method: Fabrication of CPW resonators from YBCO thin films and measurement of their microwave response (internal quality factor Q_i and fractional resonance frequency shift Δf_r/f_r) across temperatures from ~70 mK to 40 K, including microwave-power dependence studies.
AI.result: Q_i values of 4×10^3 to 10^4 at 70 mK increase to ~8×10^3–1.2×10^4 near 6 K. Low-temperature Q_i and frequency shift increase with temperature qualitatively similar to TLS behavior, but lack saturation on the resonator-frequency temperature scale and show no observable power dependence. Low-temperature frequency upturn is better fit by paramagnetic response from defect local moments or Andreev bound states; loss follows an approximately logarithmic temperature dependence of unresolved microscopic origin.
AI.conclusion: YBCO resonators operate with reasonable Q_i at millikelvin temperatures, but their low-temperature microwave response deviates from the conventional TLS model, requiring alternative microscopic explanations such as paramagnetic defects or Andreev bound states, with the low-temperature loss mechanism remaining unresolved.

title: Coordinate and Momentum Distributions of a Small Composite System
summary: An isolated small system consisting of a movable shell and a finite number of internal particles is considered. Exact distributions of the shell coordinates and momenta are obtained for various types of internal particle motion under the conditions of conservation of the total energy and momentum of the system. The coordinate distribution consists of a finite number of branches and may contain plateau regions. The momentum distribution corresponds to a non-uniform distribution of energy among the degrees of freedom of the system. It is shown that the coordinate distribution depends on the number of internal particles and remains unchanged when the dimensionality of their motion varies, whereas the momentum distribution depends on the number of degrees of freedom. Consequently, comparison of the coordinate and momentum distributions of the shell makes it possible to draw conclusions about the internal structure of the system. The chaotic motion of the shell caused by impacts from the internal particles is analyzed; unlike Brownian motion, it persists even in the absence of an external medium. A universal expression for the root-mean-square deviation of the shell is obtained explicitly, depending on the number of internal particles and their masses.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes an isolated system of a movable shell containing a finite number of internal particles. Exact coordinate and momentum distributions of the shell are derived under conservation of total energy and momentum. The coordinate distribution depends on the number of particles but not their spatial dimensionality, while the momentum distribution depends on the number of degrees of freedom. This enables inference about the internal structure via comparing both distributions. The shell exhibits chaotic motion from internal impacts even without an external medium (unlike Brownian motion), with a universal RMS deviation expression depending on particle number and masses.
AI.motivation: To understand the statistical properties of a small isolated mechanical system (a movable shell with internal particles) and determine how observations of the shell's coordinate and momentum distributions can reveal information about its hidden internal structure.
AI.method: Exact derivation of shell coordinate and momentum distributions under total energy and momentum conservation for various internal particle motions; analysis of the resulting distribution structures (finite branches, plateau regions, non-uniform energy distribution); characterization of shell's chaotic motion and derivation of a universal expression for its root-mean-square deviation.
AI.result: Coordinate distribution depends on the number of internal particles and is invariant to their motion dimensionality, while momentum distribution depends on the number of degrees of freedom. Shell exhibits persistent chaotic motion even without an external medium, distinct from Brownian motion. A universal RMS deviation expression for the shell is obtained as a function of particle number and masses.
AI.conclusion: Comparing the coordinate and momentum distributions of the shell provides a means to infer the internal structure of the system (number of particles and their degrees of freedom). The system exhibits intrinsic chaotic behavior independent of an external medium, with quantitatively predictable fluctuation statistics.

title: Harnessing Native Chromium Oxidation for Giant Orbital Torque and Field-Free Magnetization Switching in NiFe/Cr Bilayers
summary: Orbital currents offer charge-to-spin conversion beyond the efficiency limit of conventional heavy-metal Spin Hall sources. However, harnessing them has so far required either thick orbital-Hall materials or additional heavy-metal conversion layers. Here, we show that the native oxide of chromium, typically regarded as parasitic, transforms a simple NiFe\Cr bilayer into a self-contained dual-channel orbital-current source without the need for any conversion layer. First-principles calculations predict a nearly threefold enhancement of the orbital Hall conductivity upon surface oxygenation, driven by Cr(3d)-O(2p) hybridization. Experimentally, naturally oxidized NiFe\Cr heterostructures exhibit a giant damping-like torque efficiency of $3.9 \times 10^{6}$ $Ω^{-1}$ m$^{-1}$, exceeding Pt (Ta) by one (two) orders of magnitude. The torque depicts a non-monotonic Cr-thickness dependence which cannot be explained by a conventional model. We have developed a drift-diffusion model with an oxidation-gated interfacial source which quantitatively reproduces the data, revealing that the Cr-CrO$_x$ interface generates orbital currents over an order of magnitude stronger than the bulk orbital Hall channel with an orbital transport length of $\approx 4$ nm. The enhanced torque enables field-free magnetization switching at $1.58 \times 10^{11}$ A m$^{-2}$, outperforming heavy-metal and CuO$_x$ benchmarks. These results establish native oxidation as a scalable strategy for realizing efficient orbital-torque devices.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that the native oxide of chromium (CrOx) can transform a simple NiFe/Cr bilayer into a self-contained dual-channel orbital-current source, achieving a giant damping-like torque efficiency of 3.9×10^6 Ω⁻¹m⁻¹ that exceeds Pt by one order of magnitude and Ta by two orders. The oxidation-gated interfacial source generates orbital currents over an order of magnitude stronger than the bulk orbital Hall channel, enabling field-free magnetization switching at 1.58×10^11 A m⁻².
AI.motivation: Orbital currents offer charge-to-spin conversion beyond the efficiency limit of conventional heavy-metal Spin Hall sources, but harnessing them has previously required either thick orbital-Hall materials or additional heavy-metal conversion layers, limiting practical applications.
AI.method: First-principles calculations predict nearly threefold enhancement of orbital Hall conductivity upon surface oxygenation due to Cr(3d)-O(2p) hybridization. A drift-diffusion model with an oxidation-gated interfacial source was developed to quantitatively reproduce experimental torque data, revealing the Cr-CrOx interface as a strong orbital-current generator with an orbital transport length of ~4 nm.
AI.result: Naturally oxidized NiFe/Cr heterostructures exhibit a giant damping-like torque efficiency of 3.9×10^6 Ω⁻¹m⁻¹, exceeding Pt (Ta) by one (two) orders of magnitude. The Cr-CrOx interface generates orbital currents over an order of magnitude stronger than the bulk orbital Hall channel, enabling field-free magnetization switching at 1.58×10^11 A m⁻².
AI.conclusion: Native oxidation is established as a scalable strategy for realizing efficient orbital-torque devices, transforming the typically parasitic oxide into a functional source of orbital currents without requiring conversion layers.

title: Semi-supervised Hopfield model: Theoretical and Numerical results
summary: In the daily practice of Machine Learning, fully labeled datasets are a luxury: labels demand expensive and time-consuming human annotation, whereas raw, unlabeled data can be harvested automatically and in bulk. Semi-supervised learning, where the network jointly exploits the few labeled and the many unlabeled examples at its disposal, is the standard answer to this asymmetry, yet a statistical mechanical theory of semi-supervised Hebbian learning is still lacking. In this paper we fill this gap for the Hopfield network: we prescribe a synaptic coupling given by the convex combination, weighted by a mixing parameter λin [0,1], of the supervised and unsupervised Hebbian kernels built from the same archetypes, and we solve for the emergent computational capabilities of the resulting network. A signal-to-noise analysis yields the one-step Mattis magnetization and the learning threshold, i.e. the minimum dataset size for stable retrieval. Using Guerra's interpolation, we then derive the Replica Symmetric quenched pressure in the high-storage regime, treating the correlated disorder generated by the supervised and unsupervised channels through a particular eigen-channel decomposition. The resulting phase diagram shows that a mixed strategy outperforms both pure protocols. Finally, we prove that the quenched pressure is convex in λ, so thermodynamics cannot select an interior mixture: λis therefore a learning hyperparameter. All the analytical findings are successfully checked against extensive Monte Carlo simulations.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a statistical mechanical theory for semi-supervised Hebbian learning in Hopfield networks, where the synaptic coupling is a convex combination of supervised and unsupervised Hebbian kernels weighted by a mixing parameter λ. Using signal-to-noise analysis and Guerra's interpolation (with replica symmetric quenched pressure), the authors derive the learning threshold, Mattis magnetization, and phase diagram—showing mixed strategies outperform pure supervised or unsupervised protocols. The quenched pressure is proven convex in λ, meaning no interior mixture is thermodynamically selected, so λ must be treated as a hyperparameter. All results are verified against Monte Carlo simulations.
AI.motivation: Fully labeled datasets are expensive to obtain, while unlabeled data is abundant. Semi-supervised learning addresses this asymmetry, but no statistical mechanical theory exists for semi-supervised Hebbian learning, particularly in the context of Hopfield networks.
AI.method: The authors prescribe a synaptic coupling as a convex combination (weighted by λ ∈ [0,1]) of supervised and unsupervised Hebbian kernels built from the same archetypes. They employ (1) signal-to-noise analysis for one-step Mattis magnetization and learning threshold, (2) Guerra's interpolation to derive the Replica Symmetric quenched pressure in the high-storage regime, handling correlated disorder via eigen-channel decomposition, and (3) prove convexity of the quenched pressure in λ.
AI.result: The phase diagram demonstrates that a mixed (semi-supervised) strategy outperforms both pure supervised and pure unsupervised protocols. The quenched pressure is proven convex in λ, meaning thermodynamics cannot select an interior mixture—thus λ acts as a learning hyperparameter. All analytical findings are confirmed by extensive Monte Carlo simulations.
AI.conclusion: Semi-supervised Hebbian learning in Hopfield networks can be rigorously analyzed with statistical mechanics, showing performance gains from mixing supervised and unsupervised signals. Since no spontaneous thermodynamic selection of λ occurs (due to convexity), λ must be tuned as a hyperparameter in practice.

title: Spin-incoherent Mott-Thouless pumps
summary: A Thouless pump describes a system in which a quantized amount of charge is transported by one lattice spacing per cycle when the parameters of a Hamiltonian are varied slowly and periodically. In the standard case, this quantization requires the system to remain in its ground state with vanishing thermodynamic entropy throughout the pumping process. Here, we introduce a class of Mott-Thouless pumps, which operate in highly entropic, spin-incoherent Mott states. We show analytically that these states exhibit exponentially protected quantized transport despite their extensive entropy, because the pumped charge resides in a gapped sector that remains dynamically decoupled from the hot spin degrees of freedom. By contrast, motivated by a recent experimental realization, we identify other classes of Mott-Thouless pumps that lack this protection. In these systems, spin excitations can efficiently generate charge excitations, leading to a rapid breakdown of quantized transport. Our analytical results are supported by numerically exact real-time simulations of finite systems.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "Mott-Thouless pumps," a class of topological charge pumps that operate in highly entropic, spin-incoherent Mott insulating states. Despite extensive thermodynamic entropy, these systems exhibit exponentially protected quantized transport because the pumped charge resides in a gapped sector dynamically decoupled from hot spin degrees of freedom. The authors also identify unprotected Mott-Thouless pumps where spin excitations efficiently generate charge excitations, breaking quantization, and support their analytical findings with numerically exact real-time simulations of finite systems.
AI.motivation: Standard Thouless pumping requires the system to remain in its ground state with vanishing entropy. The paper aims to extend this paradigm by asking whether quantized charge transport can survive in highly entropic, thermally excited Mott insulator states, motivated by recent experimental realizations of such systems.
AI.method: The authors provide analytical arguments showing that in a certain class of Mott states, the pumped charge lives in a gapped sector dynamically decoupled from the entropic spin sector, yielding exponentially protected quantization. They contrast this with other Mott-Thouless pump classes lacking such protection, where spin excitations can seed charge excitations. The analytical results are corroborated by numerically exact real-time simulations on finite systems.
AI.result: They demonstrate that some Mott-Thouless pumps exhibit exponentially protected quantized charge transport even at extensive entropy, while other classes, motivated by recent experiments, undergo rapid breakdown of quantization due to spin-charge coupling. Both results are confirmed by numerically exact real-time simulations.
AI.conclusion: Quantized Thouless charge transport is possible even in highly entropic Mott insulating states, provided the charge sector is gapped and dynamically decoupled from the entropic spin sector. This expands the realm of topological pumping beyond ground-state physics and clarifies the conditions under which such protection holds or fails.

title: Performance Benchmarking: Software for the Density Matrix Renormalization Group
summary: The performance of scientific software often determines the scale of problems that can be solved in practice. As multiple implementations of the same algorithm emerge, systematic evaluation is needed to compare their strengths and limitations. The density matrix renormalization group (DMRG) algorithm, widely used to study quantum systems, has over 50 software implementations. These implementations vary in multiple aspects that can strongly affect performance. However, despite the need, performance evaluations of these implementations are scarce and lack a consistent standard; many existing evaluations are either too incomplete to enable meaningful comparisons or focus on objectives other than direct performance comparisons, thereby limiting understanding of how the implementations compare. Here, we present a performance-oriented benchmarking framework to facilitate meaningful comparisons of DMRG implementations, and we apply it to quantify the performance of eight implementations, highlighting similarities and differences among them. Furthermore, we examine multiple parameter settings, optimization strategies, and implementation-specific features to demonstrate how parameter configuration can affect performance and how systematic evaluation can reveal non-obvious trade-offs. The results show significant performance differences, up to two orders of magnitude in some cases, not only between different implementations when aligning parameters, but also within the same implementation when comparing different parameter configurations. Hence, our results demonstrate the significant value and insight that can be gained from conducting rigorous performance evaluations. Using our results and framework as a starting point, more rigorous benchmarking will ultimately help users and developers make informed decisions and support future development efforts to build better, more efficient software.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a performance-oriented benchmarking framework for DMRG (density matrix renormalization group) software implementations and applies it to eight different implementations, revealing performance differences up to two orders of magnitude both across implementations and across parameter configurations within the same implementation.
AI.motivation: With over 50 DMRG software implementations available, performance evaluations are scarce and lack a consistent standard. Existing evaluations are either too incomplete for meaningful comparisons or focus on objectives other than direct performance comparisons, limiting understanding of how these implementations compare.
AI.method: The authors develop a performance-oriented benchmarking framework for DMRG implementations and apply it to eight implementations. They systematically examine multiple parameter settings, optimization strategies, and implementation-specific features to quantify performance and reveal trade-offs.
AI.result: The benchmarks show significant performance differences—up to two orders of magnitude in some cases—both between different implementations when parameters are aligned, and within the same implementation across different parameter configurations.
AI.conclusion: Rigorous performance evaluations provide significant value and insight. The framework and results serve as a foundation for more rigorous benchmarking, helping users and developers make informed decisions and supporting future development of more efficient DMRG software.

title: MatCreatioNN: Machine learning-guided computational discovery of photocatalysts for environmental applications
comment: 8 figures, 0 tables. Supplementary information attached to file and data (Zenodo, Github) available
summary: The rational design of photocatalysts for environmental remediation and CO2 conversion remains limited by the high computational cost and sparse experimental data describing multi-parameter photocatalytic behavior. This work presents an integrated machine-learning framework that couples reinforcement learning-based metal-organic framework (MOF) generation with a multi-stage Crystal Graph Convolutional Neural Network (CGCNN) prediction funnel to identify photocatalysts optimized across multiple electronic and structural features. 120,000 MOF candidates were generated and screened using 13 key descriptors, including band-gap suitability, CO2/H2O selectivity, adsorption energy, and structural stability. The funnel approach reduced computational cost by 4.13-fold while maintaining predictive robustness. Two top candidates, a Cr-based and a Zn-based MOF, exhibited predicted photocatalytic fitness values of 1.70 +/- 0.25 and 1.20 +/- 0.05 fold higher respectively than benchmark materials such as PCN-224(Zr), demonstrating simultaneous improvements in light absorption, redox energetics, and framework durability. Simulated X-ray diffraction patterns confirmed strong structural agreement with experimentally synthesized MOFs, indicating high synthesizability. Post-hoc analysis revealed recurring structural motifs, such as the N262 metal cluster, that correlated strongly with high predicted photocatalytic activity. These results highlight the potential of data-driven methods to accelerate discovery of efficient and durable photocatalysts for environmental and energy-related transformations, providing a foundation for experimental realization and large-scale implementation of computationally designed MOFs.

AI.tldr: This work introduces an integrated machine-learning framework combining reinforcement learning-based MOF generation with a multi-stage CGCNN prediction funnel to accelerate photocatalyst discovery. Screening 120,000 MOF candidates across 13 descriptors with 4.13-fold computational cost reduction, the framework identified Cr- and Zn-based MOFs outperforming benchmarks like PCN-224(Zr) by 1.20–1.70× in photocatalytic fitness, with simulated XRD confirming synthesizability.
AI.motivation: Rational design of photocatalysts is limited by high computational costs and sparse experimental data when considering the multi-parameter nature of photocatalytic behavior for environmental remediation and CO2 conversion.
AI.method: A dual-component framework: (1) reinforcement learning for generative MOF design, and (2) a multi-stage Crystal Graph Convolutional Neural Network (CGCNN) prediction funnel for screening candidates using 13 key descriptors (band-gap, CO2/H2O selectivity, adsorption energy, structural stability, etc.).
AI.result: 120,000 MOF candidates generated and screened; 4.13-fold reduction in computational cost. Top candidates (Cr-based and Zn-based MOFs) achieved photocatalytic fitness values 1.20–1.70× higher than PCN-224(Zr) benchmarks. Simulated XRD patterns confirmed structural agreement with synthesized MOFs, and post-hoc analysis identified the N262 metal cluster as a recurring high-activity motif.
AI.conclusion: Data-driven generative and predictive methods can substantially accelerate the discovery of efficient, durable photocatalysts, offering a foundation for experimental realization and large-scale implementation of computationally designed MOFs for environmental and energy applications.

title: Storing Sensor Events in the Interconnection Strength of Conducting Polymer Dendrites
summary: If electronics drives only electrons to charge electrodes, natural systems learn by moving matter to evolve. Morphogenesis in sessile organisms can be seen both as a fabrication process and as an operative mechanism. However, intricating manufacturing and programming functionalities in electronic hardware is not conventional. In this study, we experimentally implement such a concept of an evolutionary electrical system using a neuro-inspired electronic nose as a model, to store a history of sensory data in the physical properties of the electrical interconnects of sensing elements. Triggered only by volatile molecule exposures, different sensing elements change instantaneously and reversibly their impedance, so pulse voltages enable the electrochemical growth of conducting polymer dendrites. The strength of the evolving interconnects is specific to the sensing materials and to the nature of volatile molecules to which they are exposed. The dendritic growths occur exclusively when exposed to volatile samples, and stop immediately after interrupting the exposure. The capability of such "passive memory" was also assessed by simulating a network architecture, which showed that this way of storing information should greatly diminish the fabrication complexity of a highly dense sensing array while realistically enabling its calibration to classify user-specific environment exposures. By demonstrating that memory in electronics can be a concept linked to manufacturing like in living organisms, this study shows that low material resources and low energy activation can be exploited for practical electronic applications in future-emerging sensing technologies.

AI.tldr: This study experimentally implements an evolutionary electrical system using a neuro-inspired electronic nose, where volatile molecule exposures trigger electrochemical growth of conducting polymer dendrites on sensing elements, storing a history of sensory data in the physical properties of electrical interconnects—demonstrating that memory can be linked to manufacturing, resembling morphogenesis in living organisms.
AI.motivation: Natural systems learn by moving matter to evolve, whereas conventional electronics only drive electrons to charge electrodes. The authors aim to challenge the convention of separating manufacturing from programming functionalities in electronic hardware, by intricating fabrication and computing—an approach inspired by morphogenesis in sessile organisms.
AI.method: Using a neuro-inspired electronic nose as a model, sensing elements undergo instantaneous and reversible impedance changes upon volatile molecule exposure. Pulse voltages trigger electrochemical growth of conducting polymer dendrites, with growth strength being specific to the sensing material and the nature of the volatile molecules. The dendritic growth occurs exclusively during exposure and stops immediately upon interruption. Additionally, network architecture simulations were performed to assess the capability of this passive memory.
AI.result: The evolving interconnects grow dendrites selectively in response to volatile samples, ceasing growth when exposure stops. Simulations showed that this passive memory storage approach greatly diminishes the fabrication complexity of a highly dense sensing array while realistically enabling calibration to classify user-specific environment exposures.
AI.conclusion: Memory in electronics can be a concept linked to manufacturing, analogous to living organisms. This demonstrates that low material resources and low energy activation can be exploited for practical electronic applications in future-emerging sensing technologies.

title: Vibe-FDTR: An agent-oriented framework for reproducible frequency-domain thermoreflectance data analysis
summary: Frequency-domain thermoreflectance (FDTR) is a laser pump-probe technique widely used to measure thermal properties at the micro- and nanoscale; however, it relies on a complex data analysis procedure that demands substantial domain expertise and is susceptible to subtle human errors. Here, we present Vibe-FDTR, an agent-oriented framework that enables large language model (LLM) agents to perform reliable and reproducible FDTR analyses directly from natural language requests. This framework couples a configuration-driven FDTR code package, which enforces physical and parametric consistency, with procedural agent skills that translate user intentions into organized and verifiable analysis steps. We evaluate Vibe-FDTR using a controlled benchmark with two levels: synthetic single-step tasks and real-data multi-step tasks based on measurements of gold-coated graphite samples. Across the two levels, agents using Vibe-FDTR achieve success rates of 100% and 98.9%, respectively. In sharp contrast, ablating skills (Code-agent) reduces performance to 91.4% and 36.7%, which drops further to 38.6% and 0% when the domain package is also omitted (Agent-only). Beyond success rate, Vibe-FDTR also reduces computational cost by 87.7% relative to the Code-agent variant and cuts execution time by more than 60%. Finally, an optional expert mode supports experimental planning via autonomous sensitivity and uncertainty evaluations, and formulates physically grounded recommendations for underspecified tasks. These results demonstrate that encapsulating domain code and expert knowledge into agent skills offers a promising route toward low-barrier, autonomous, and trustworthy thermal metrology.

AI.tldr: Vibe-FDTR is an agent-oriented framework that enables large language model (LLM) agents to perform reliable and reproducible frequency-domain thermoreflectance (FDTR) analyses from natural language requests, achieving 100% and 98.9% success rates on synthetic single-step and real-data multi-step benchmark tasks, respectively, while reducing computational cost by 87.7% and execution time by over 60% compared to ablation variants.
AI.motivation: FDTR is a widely used laser pump-probe technique for measuring micro- and nanoscale thermal properties, but its data analysis is complex, requires substantial domain expertise, and is susceptible to subtle human errors. The authors aim to lower this barrier by enabling autonomous, reliable, and reproducible FDTR analyses.
AI.method: The framework couples a configuration-driven FDTR code package that enforces physical and parametric consistency with procedural agent skills that translate natural language user intentions into organized and verifiable analysis steps. It was evaluated on a two-level benchmark (synthetic single-step and real-data multi-step tasks) using comparisons against ablated variants (Code-agent without skills and Agent-only without both skills and domain package). An optional expert mode uses autonomous sensitivity and uncertainty evaluations to support experimental planning.
AI.result: Vibe-FDTR achieved 100% success on synthetic single-step tasks and 98.9% on real-data multi-step tasks. Ablating skills (Code-agent) reduced performance to 91.4% and 36.7%, while omitting both skills and the domain package (Agent-only) further dropped results to 38.6% and 0%. Vibe-FDTR also reduced computational cost by 87.7% and execution time by more than 60% compared to the Code-agent variant.
AI.conclusion: Encapsulating domain code and expert knowledge into agent skills offers a promising route toward low-barrier, autonomous, and trustworthy thermal metrology, with Vibe-FDTR demonstrating high reliability, efficiency, and expert-level planning capabilities.

title: Extended s-wave superconductivity in M-point twisted bilayer SnSe2
summary: We investigate the emergence of electronic order and unconventional superconductivity in M-valley moiré materials. Starting from a first-principles Wannier model of AB-stacked twisted SnSe2, we tackle the (gate-screened) long-ranged Coulomb interaction with functional renormalization group simulations resolving the momentum structure and energy scales of the leading Fermi surface instabilities. Upon doping an antiferromagnetic stripe state at half-filling ($ν=3$ electrons per moiré unit cell) of the moiré flat bands, magnetic order gives way to unconventional superconductivity mediated by valley-selective spin fluctuations: Large hole doping ($ν\approx1$) leads to weak-coupling superconductors with various pairing symmetries, while slight electron- and hole-doping ($ν\approx2,4$) stabilizes a spin-singlet, extended s-wave state that benefits from scattering between virtual particle and hole states that are detuned from the Fermi level. These findings establish M-point moiré materials as a quantum simulation platform with phenomenological parallels to the class of iron pnictide superconductors.

AI.tldr: This paper studies electronic order and unconventional superconductivity in M-valley moiré materials (specifically twisted SnSe2) using functional renormalization group simulations with a first-principles Wannier model and gate-screened long-ranged Coulomb interactions. Depending on doping, the system transitions from an antiferromagnetic stripe state to various unconventional superconducting phases, including weak-coupling superconductors with different pairing symmetries at large hole doping and an extended s-wave state near half-filling, establishing these materials as a platform analogous to iron pnictide superconductors.
AI.motivation: To investigate the emergence of electronic order and unconventional superconductivity in M-valley moiré materials, a relatively underexplored class of moiré systems compared to K-valley counterparts, and to determine the nature of Fermi surface instabilities arising from long-ranged Coulomb interactions.
AI.method: First-principles Wannier modeling of AB-stacked twisted SnSe2 combined with functional renormalization group (fRG) simulations that resolve momentum structure and energy scales of leading Fermi surface instabilities, including gate-screened long-ranged Coulomb interactions.
AI.result: Upon doping an antiferromagnetic stripe state at half-filling (ν=3), magnetic order gives way to unconventional superconductivity mediated by valley-selective spin fluctuations. Large hole doping (ν≈1) yields weak-coupling superconductors with various pairing symmetries, while slight electron/hole doping (ν≈2,4) stabilizes a spin-singlet extended s-wave state arising from scattering between virtual particle and hole states detuned from the Fermi level.
AI.conclusion: M-point moiré materials serve as a quantum simulation platform with phenomenological parallels to iron pnictide superconductors, exhibiting a rich doping-dependent phase diagram of magnetic order and unconventional superconductivity.

title: When trajectory-based bounds fail: information thermodynamics under noisy feedback
summary: Information engines exploit feedback to extract work from thermal fluctuations, extending the second law of thermodynamics through information-theoretic bounds. While several such bounds have been proposed, their relative performance under realistic conditions---where measurements are noisy and feedback is temporally correlated---remains largely unclear. Here, we experimentally and theoretically investigate this problem in an underdamped feedback-controlled system with Markovian measurements but non-Markovian control sequences. We compare three representative bounds derived from transfer entropy, unavailable information, and Markovian mutual information, and find that none is universally optimal. Instead, measurement noise preferentially affects information measures that rely on detailed trajectory statistics, while leaving quantities based on instantaneous correlations comparatively robust. As a consequence, trajectory-dependent bounds deteriorate rapidly, giving rise to a crossover in which the Markovian mutual-information bound becomes tighter than the unavailable-information bound over a broad range of measurement noise. Our results reveal a general limitation of information-theoretic descriptions that rely on detailed trajectory statistics in realistic settings and provide a unified perspective on information thermodynamics beyond idealised feedback protocols.

AI.tldr: This paper experimentally and theoretically investigates three information-theoretic bounds (transfer entropy, unavailable information, and Markovian mutual information) for work extraction in underdamped feedback-controlled systems under realistic conditions with noisy measurements and non-Markovian control. None of the bounds is universally optimal; measurement noise degrades trajectory-statistics-based bounds while leaving instantaneous-correlation-based measures relatively robust, leading to a crossover where Markovian mutual information becomes tighter than unavailable information across a broad noise range.
AI.motivation: Information engines extend the second law via information-theoretic bounds, but their relative performance under realistic conditions—noisy measurements and temporally correlated feedback—remains unclear. The authors aim to clarify how these bounds behave and whether any is universally superior.
AI.method: The authors combine experiments and theory on an underdamped feedback-controlled system with Markovian measurements but non-Markovian control sequences, comparing three representative information-theoretic bounds: transfer entropy, unavailable information, and Markovian mutual information.
AI.result: None of the three bounds is universally optimal. Measurement noise preferentially degrades information measures relying on detailed trajectory statistics while leaving instantaneous-correlation-based measures comparatively robust. This causes trajectory-dependent bounds to deteriorate rapidly, producing a crossover where Markovian mutual-information bound becomes tighter than unavailable-information bound over a wide range of measurement noise.
AI.conclusion: The results reveal a general limitation of information-theoretic descriptions that depend on detailed trajectory statistics in realistic settings, and provide a unified perspective on information thermodynamics beyond idealized feedback protocols.

title: Fluctuation electrodynamics of quantum capacitance in electron bilayers
summary: Capacitance is a thermodynamic probe of interacting electrons: it measures the energy cost of moving charge between conductors, and in low-dimensional systems this cost is shaped by exchange and correlation as much as by electrostatics. We develop a theory of the quantum capacitance of electron double layers, semiconductor quantum wells as well as monolayer and bilayer graphene devices, focusing on the contribution generated by interlayer correlations. Within a functional-integral formulation we show that the separation-dependent part of the ground-state energy is, at the level of ring diagrams, exactly the nonretarded Lifshitz expression for the van der Waals energy of two conducting sheets, with reflection amplitudes built from the layer polarizabilities. The interlayer correction to the inverse capacitance is the second density derivative of this energy: a Casimir compressibility. The zero-point fluctuations that generate Casimir forces between mirrors are here the coupled plasmons of the bilayer, and their contribution to the capacitance is obtained in closed form, with a universal coefficient; its sign shows that interlayer correlations oppose charging at high density. A Gell-Mann-Brueckner analysis gives the exact high-density limit in terms of universal functions. For graphene we find that monolayers follow the electron-gas template, while bilayer graphene is anomalous: interband screening suppresses the correction by orders of magnitude and reverses its sign in the experimentally relevant range of separations. We delineate the limits of the theory, identifying the dilute Wigner-crystal regime and electron-hole double layers near exciton condensation as regimes where the capacitance becomes a probe of interlayer pairing.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a theory of quantum capacitance in electron double layers, semiconductor quantum wells, and monolayer/bilayer graphene devices, showing that interlayer correlations contribute a Casimir-like compressibility term derived from the van der Waals energy. The correction is computed in closed form with a universal coefficient at the ring-diagram level, and the authors find that bilayer graphene behaves anomalously due to interband screening.
AI.motivation: To understand how interlayer correlations—exchange and correlation effects beyond electrostatics—shape the quantum capacitance of low-dimensional electron systems, and to establish a theoretical framework that connects capacitance to interlayer pairing phenomena.
AI.method: A functional-integral formulation is used to show that the separation-dependent ground-state energy equals the nonretarded Lifshitz expression for van der Waals energy at the ring-diagram level, with reflection amplitudes built from layer polarizabilities. A Gell-Mann-Brueckner analysis provides the exact high-density limit, and closed-form results for the Casimir compressibility are derived from coupled plasmon zero-point fluctuations.
AI.result: The interlayer correction to inverse capacitance takes the form of a Casimir compressibility with a universal coefficient, and its sign indicates interlayer correlations oppose charging at high density. Monolayer graphene follows the electron-gas template, but bilayer graphene is anomalous: interband screening suppresses the correction by orders of magnitude and reverses its sign in experimentally relevant separation ranges.
AI.conclusion: The theory delineates its limits, identifying dilute Wigner-crystal regimes and electron-hole double layers near exciton condensation as regimes where capacitance becomes a probe of interlayer pairing. The framework unifies Casimir physics and quantum capacitance through coupled plasmon fluctuations.

title: Quantum Chaos and Diffusive Transport from Geometric Randomness
summary: The physics of quantum chaos and diffusive transport is typically studied in settings with microscopic disorder or many-body interactions. In this Letter, we demonstrate that these phenomena can arise purely from geometric randomness. By studying non-interacting quantum particles on random locally tree-like layered graphs with uniform couplings, we show that the geometric randomness and effective graph dimensionality dictates the presence of chaotic dynamics or lack thereof. These graphs can be considered as structurally disordered generalisations of regular square lattices or ladders, or equivalently as multi-component one-dimensional chains with random links between the components. We find that an extensive layer size yields robust quantum chaos, level repulsion, and diffusive transport. Conversely, in the quasi-one-dimensional limit, we find the coexistence of extensive number of localised and delocalised states -- this leads to suppressed level repulsion accompanied by the latter driving ballistic transport. These results establish geometric randomness as a fundamental and independent mechanism for generating and tuning quantum chaos.

AI.tldr: This Letter demonstrates that quantum chaos and diffusive transport can emerge purely from geometric randomness, without microscopic disorder or many-body interactions. Using non-interacting quantum particles on random locally tree-like layered graphs with uniform couplings, the authors show that extensive layer size produces robust quantum chaos, level repulsion, and diffusive transport, while the quasi-one-dimensional limit exhibits coexisting localized and delocalized states with suppressed level repulsion and ballistic transport.
AI.motivation: Quantum chaos and diffusive transport are conventionally studied in systems with microscopic disorder or many-body interactions. This work challenges that paradigm by asking whether purely geometric randomness—structural disorder in the graph connectivity itself—can independently generate these phenomena, establishing a new fundamental mechanism for quantum chaos.
AI.method: The authors study non-interacting quantum particles on random locally tree-like layered graphs with uniform couplings. These graphs serve as structurally disordered generalizations of regular square lattices or ladders, equivalently viewed as multi-component one-dimensional chains with random links between components. They analyze the system by varying the layer size, spanning from extensive to quasi-one-dimensional limits, and examine signatures of quantum chaos including level statistics, level repulsion, and transport properties.
AI.result: An extensive layer size yields robust quantum chaos, level repulsion, and diffusive transport. In the quasi-one-dimensional limit, a coexistence of an extensive number of localized and delocalized states is found, which suppresses level repulsion while the delocalized states drive ballistic transport.
AI.conclusion: Geometric randomness is established as a fundamental and independent mechanism for generating and tuning quantum chaos, independent of microscopic disorder or many-body interactions.

title: Altermagnetism from a Cu-Fe Lieb Lattice in FeSe/Cuprate Heterostructures
summary: Realizing altermagnetism in high-$T_c$ cuprate-based systems would provide a direct route for studying spin-split electronic bands in the absence of net magnetization and investigate their interplay with unconventional superconductivity. Here, we propose that FeSe/cuprate heterostructures offer such a platform, where a 45$^\circ$ twist of Cu and Fe layers creates an effective CuFe$_2$ Lieb lattice in which Fe magnetic order and Cu-Fe hybridization through the ligands induces altermagnetic $d$-wave spin splitting. A minimal tight-binding model shows that this mechanism is generic. Furthermore, a substrate-induced inequivalence of the two Se sites in FeSe provides a second route in which altermagnetism originates in the Fe layer and is transferred to the cuprate layer by proximity. Density functional theory calculations for FeSe/Bi$_2$Sr$_2$CuO$_6$ heterostructures confirm the viability of both mechanisms and reveal ways to enhance the spin splitting. These results establish superconducting cuprate/transition metal chalcogenide heterostructures as a promising setting for engineering altermagnetism and studying its coupling to unconventional superconductivity.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes FeSe/cuprate heterostructures as a platform for realizing altermagnetism—spin-split electronic bands without net magnetization—in high-Tc cuprate systems. Two mechanisms are identified: (1) a 45° twist between Cu and Fe layers creating a CuFe2 Lieb lattice with d-wave altermagnetic spin splitting via hybridization, and (2) substrate-induced Se-site inequivalence generating altermagnetism in the Fe layer that transfers to the cuprate via proximity. DFT calculations confirm both mechanisms in FeSe/Bi2Sr2CuO6 heterostructures, establishing cuprate/chalcogenide interfaces as promising for studying altermagnetism coupled to unconventional superconductivity.
AI.motivation: To enable the study of spin-split electronic bands (altermagnetism) in high-Tc cuprate-based systems in the absence of net magnetization, and to investigate how altermagnetism interacts with unconventional superconductivity.
AI.method: The paper combines a minimal tight-binding model to demonstrate the generic nature of the altermagnetic d-wave spin-splitting mechanism, and density functional theory (DFT) calculations for FeSe/Bi2Sr2CuO6 heterostructures to validate both proposed mechanisms—the twisted CuFe2 Lieb lattice route and the Se-site inequivalence route.
AI.result: Both mechanisms for realizing altermagnetism in FeSe/cuprate heterostructures are confirmed viable. The tight-binding model shows the mechanism is generic, and DFT calculations for FeSe/Bi2Sr2CuO6 confirm both routes and reveal strategies to enhance the spin splitting.
AI.conclusion: Superconducting cuprate/transition metal chalcogenide heterostructures represent a promising platform for engineering altermagnetism and studying its coupling to unconventional superconductivity.

title: Fast and Accurate Foundation Models for Equivariant Machine-Learned Interatomic Potentials
summary: Machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) have emerged as a transformative tool for computational materials science and chemistry, with universal potentials trained on large and diverse datasets now routinely deployed as 'foundation models' for downstream fine-tuning in targeted chemical spaces. Many scientific applications of the resulting models, such as molecular dynamics (MD), require high inference and training speeds as well as accuracy. In this work, we examine the limits of equivariant MLIPs, which directly encode physical symmetries in model architectures, to achieve these competing targets -- particularly in the regime of extremely large datasets where data efficiency is less critical. We show how this trade-off can be addressed, and present a family of foundation potentials in the NequIP and Allegro equivariant MLIP architectures which achieve leading inference speeds and strong scalability as well as excellent accuracies across a range of community benchmarks -- spanning materials discovery, thermal conductivity prediction, and near-equilibrium mechanical and thermodynamic properties. Accelerations implemented within the NequIP infrastructure now permit training of high-accuracy foundation potentials on ultra-large datasets with dramatically reduced computational cost. Alongside, we show that efforts to improve model accuracy for materials discovery should focus on dataset diversity and improved, consistent descriptions of transition metal compound energy surfaces.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a family of equivariant MLIP foundation models based on the NequIP and Allegro architectures that achieve leading inference speeds, strong scalability, and excellent accuracy across multiple community benchmarks, with accelerated training on ultra-large datasets.
AI.motivation: Many scientific applications (e.g., molecular dynamics) require MLIPs to achieve both high inference/training speeds and accuracy simultaneously. Universal foundation potentials need to be fine-tuned downstream, and there is a trade-off between expressive equivariant architectures and computational performance—especially in the large-data regime where data efficiency matters less.
AI.method: The authors examine the limits of equivariant MLIP architectures (NequIP and Allegro) that encode physical symmetries directly, and introduce computational optimizations/accelerations within the NequIP infrastructure to reduce the cost of training high-accuracy foundation potentials on ultra-large datasets.
AI.result: The resulting foundation potentials achieve leading inference speeds, strong scalability, and excellent accuracy across benchmarks in materials discovery, thermal conductivity prediction, and near-equilibrium mechanical/thermodynamic properties. Training on ultra-large datasets is enabled with dramatically reduced computational cost.
AI.conclusion: For materials discovery, improving model accuracy should prioritize dataset diversity and more consistent descriptions of transition metal compound energy surfaces, rather than solely architectural improvements.

title: Parity-selective spin splitting in coplanar antiferromagnets via bichromatic driving
summary: Parity is a central characteristic of momentum-dependent spin splitting in antiferromagnets (AFMs). Yet, intrinsic crystal symmetries typically restrict the splitting to either even or odd parity, preventing flexible spin control. Using a coplanar AFM, we demonstrate that bichromatic ($ω$--$nω$) Floquet driving offers a natural way to bypass this constraint. This mechanism generates asymmetric spin textures unattainable in static AFMs or under monochromatic driving. For the specific AFM considered here, we reveal an elegant relation between spin-splitting parity and harmonic hierarchy: $ω$--$2ω$ fields generate highly tunable odd- and mixed-parity spin splittings, whereas higher-order harmonics ($n \ge 3$) exclusively produce even-parity states. The macroscopic magnetization can also be toggled via the specific driving protocol and harmonic $n$. These distinct spin splitting states manifest in qualitatively different macroscopic spin currents generated after an optical quench---a definitive transport signature complementing direct visualization via spin- and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that bichromatic (ω–nω) Floquet driving of a coplanar antiferromagnet can bypass the intrinsic parity restriction of momentum-dependent spin splitting, generating asymmetric spin textures and tunable odd/mixed/even-parity spin splittings that are impossible in static or monochromatically driven systems.
AI.motivation: Parity is a key attribute of momentum-dependent spin splitting in antiferromagnets, but intrinsic crystal symmetries usually lock the splitting to either even or odd parity, limiting flexible spin control. The authors seek a natural mechanism to overcome this constraint.
AI.method: Using bichromatic Floquet driving (ω–nω) on a coplanar antiferromagnet, the authors analyze how the harmonic hierarchy (choice of n) controls the parity of the resulting spin-split states, and compute macroscopic spin currents generated after an optical quench as a transport signature.
AI.result: ω–2ω driving produces highly tunable odd- and mixed-parity spin splittings, while higher harmonics (n≥3) exclusively generate even-parity states. Macroscopic magnetization can be toggled via the driving protocol and harmonic choice. Distinct spin-splitting states yield qualitatively different macroscopic spin currents after an optical quench, providing a transport signature complementary to spin- and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy.
AI.conclusion: Bichromatic Floquet driving provides a natural and flexible route to control spin-splitting parity in antiferromagnets, enabling spin textures and transport signatures unattainable in static systems or under monochromatic driving.

title: A Quantum Mechanical Approach to the Computation of Rovibrational Spectra of Diatomic Molecules in Strong Magnetic Fields
summary: In the absence of experimental data for molecular spectra in strong magnetic fields, high resolution and reliable computational spectra are required for the interpretation of spectra collected from highly magnetic astrophysical objects. In this paper, we extend the Wilson-Hamiltonian framework, recently implemented and benchmarked by us (\textit{J. Chem. Theory Comput.}, \textbf{21}, 9753 (2025) ), to a general three-dimensional framework suitable for computing the rovibrational spectra of diatomic molecules in strong uniform magnetic fields. The field-dependent electronic and nuclear Hamiltonians capture full non-perturbative coupling between particle motion and the field making the method applicable to all field strengths. The electric quadrupole transition moment integrals for rovibrational transitions in external static magnetic fields are formulated, implemented, and computed to yield spectra which respect the selection rules of the molecule-field system. The spectral changes with increasing field strength such as shifting, splitting, merging, appearance and disappearance of peaks are noted. Contributions from electrons and nuclei are studied individually, as well as in unison to reveal the underlying physics such as stiffening of the bond, emergence of a rotational barrier, field-induced coupling/decoupling of states, and symmetry-breaking in rotational and vibrational states. These results provide the first fully quantum mechanical computational results for the rovibrational signature of $^1\mathrm{H}_{2}$ in extreme magnetic field environments with accuracy suitable for experimental interpretation. The methodology developed herein has direct relevance for high-field spectroscopy and astrochemical modeling, both for providing computational data as well as for understanding the spectral impact of strong magnetic fields on electronic structure and nuclear motion in molecules.

AI.tldr: This paper extends the Wilson-Hamiltonian framework to a fully three-dimensional formalism for computing rovibrational spectra of diatomic molecules in strong uniform magnetic fields, including field-dependent electronic and nuclear Hamiltonians with non-perturbative coupling, electric quadrupole transition moment integrals, and the first quantum mechanical rovibrational spectra of ^1H2 in extreme magnetic fields showing spectral changes like shifting, splitting, merging, and symmetry-breaking.
AI.motivation: Experimental data for molecular spectra in strong magnetic fields is unavailable, so reliable computational spectra are required to interpret observations from highly magnetic astrophysical objects.
AI.method: Extends the previously benchmarked Wilson-Hamiltonian framework to a general 3D framework. Uses field-dependent electronic and nuclear Hamiltonians capturing full non-perturbative particle-field coupling applicable to all field strengths. Formulates and implements electric quadrupole transition moment integrals for rovibrational transitions in external static magnetic fields.
AI.result: Computes rovibrational spectra revealing spectral changes with increasing field strength including shifting, splitting, merging, appearance/disappearance of peaks. Contributions from electrons and nuclei are analyzed separately and together, revealing physics such as bond stiffening, rotational barriers, field-induced state coupling/decoupling, and symmetry-breaking. Provides the first fully quantum mechanical rovibrational spectra of ^1H2 in extreme magnetic fields.
AI.conclusion: The methodology is directly relevant to high-field spectroscopy and astrochemical modeling, providing computational data and understanding of strong magnetic field effects on electronic structure and nuclear motion in molecules.

title: Matching Trace Element Distribution to Mineralogical Phases in Ancient Biotechnology-Derived Metallic Salts: a Multimodal Analysis
summary: Conventional X-ray fluorescence (XRF) and X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis applied to the investigation of ancient metal salts used as pigments and/or therapeutics provide bulk average compositions in two stand-alone data sets; however, major elements aside, these two sets cannot inform on the spatial distribution of one with respect to the other. To address this issue, we present here a multimodal approach incorporating spatially resolved XRF, XRD and nanoscale X-ray imaging applied to the analysis of archaeological and experimental samples of synthetic lead carbonate (PbCO3 - Greek psimythion); psimythion was used in antiquity as a cosmetic and/or a therapeutic for external applications. The experimental sample was produced according to a well-documented recipe dated to the 4th century BCE. In this paper we demonstrate that by using a multimodal approach we can confidently assign trace elements to individual crystalline or to infer the existence of non-crystalline phases. Although the assignment of an element to a phase (i.e. the location) is now possible, the origin underlying it (i.e. the mechanism) is not always clear. Trace elements do not 'control' chemical/mineralogical composition, but they can influence it. Our approach is particularly suited to following changes in the artefact's chemical/mineralogical profile, from its manufacture, to use and burial, to excavation and conservation.

AI.tldr: The authors present a multimodal approach combining spatially resolved XRF, XRD, and nanoscale X-ray imaging to analyze archaeological and experimental samples of synthetic lead carbonate (psimythion), enabling confident assignment of trace elements to individual crystalline phases or inference of non-crystalline phases in ancient metal salts.
AI.motivation: Conventional bulk XRF and XRD analyses of ancient metal salts provide separate compositional and structural datasets but cannot correlate the spatial distribution of elements with phases. This limits understanding of the chemical/mineralogical history of pigment/therapeutic materials like psimythion.
AI.method: A multimodal approach incorporating spatially resolved X-ray fluorescence (XRF), X-ray diffraction (XRD), and nanoscale X-ray imaging was applied to archaeological samples and an experimental sample of synthetic lead carbonate (PbCO3) produced according to a 4th century BCE recipe.
AI.result: The multimodal approach allows confident assignment of trace elements to individual crystalline phases and inference of non-crystalline phases. Trace element-to-phase assignment (location) is now possible, though the underlying origin/mechanism is not always clear; trace elements do not control but can influence chemical/mineralogical composition.
AI.conclusion: The approach is particularly well-suited to tracking changes in an artefact's chemical/mineralogical profile across its life cycle — from manufacture, to use, burial, excavation, and conservation.

title: Single-crystal structural phase diagram of stoichiometric bilayer nickelate La3Ni2O7 under hydrostatic pressure
summary: The bilayer nickelate La3Ni2O7 has attracted intense interest following the discovery of high-temperature superconductivity under pressure, representing the first nickelate superconductor realized in bulk form. However, the crystal structure of the superconducting phase remains under active discussion, complicating efforts to establish its microscopic origin. Here we resolve these structural controversies by establishing a definitive pressure-temperature phase diagram, including the superconducting region of stoichiometric La3Ni2O7 single crystals under hydrostatic conditions using helium as the pressure-transmitting medium. At ambient pressure, La3Ni2O7 adopts a polar orthorhombic Am2m structure characterized by charge order between inequivalent Ni sites and NiO6 octahedral tilting. Upon compression, the system undergoes a direct transition from the charge-ordered Am2m phase to the tetragonal I4/mmm phase near 10 GPa, coinciding with the onset of bulk superconductivity. These results establish the intrinsic structural evolution of La3Ni2O7 and provide a structural framework for microscopic theories of nickelate superconductivity.

AI.tldr: This paper resolves structural controversies in the bilayer nickelate superconductor La3Ni2O7 by establishing a definitive pressure-temperature phase diagram using hydrostatic conditions with helium as the pressure medium. It shows a direct structural transition from a charge-ordered polar orthorhombic Am2m phase to a tetragonal I4/mmm phase near 10 GPa, coinciding with the onset of bulk superconductivity.
AI.motivation: The crystal structure of the superconducting phase of La3Ni2O7 remains under active discussion, which complicates efforts to establish the microscopic origin of its high-temperature superconductivity. A definitive structural framework is needed.
AI.method: Establishment of a pressure-temperature phase diagram for stoichiometric La3Ni2O7 single crystals under hydrostatic conditions using helium as the pressure-transmitting medium, with structural characterization via diffraction.
AI.result: At ambient pressure, La3Ni2O7 adopts a polar orthorhombic Am2m structure with charge order between inequivalent Ni sites and NiO6 octahedral tilting. Under compression, a direct transition from the charge-ordered Am2m phase to the tetragonal I4/mmm phase occurs near 10 GPa, coinciding with the onset of bulk superconductivity.
AI.conclusion: The results establish the intrinsic structural evolution of La3Ni2O7 and provide a structural framework for microscopic theories of nickelate superconductivity.

title: From pink to brown: Interaction-driven noise color shift in the Aubry-Andr{é} Model
summary: We revisit the metal-insulator transition in a one-dimensional lattice subjected to an on-site quasiperiodic potential, modeled using spin-1/2 particles with tunable nearest-neighbor interactions. To characterize the transition, we examine the power-spectrum, defined as the squared modulus of the Fourier transform of consecutive level spacings. In the absence of interactions, the power-spectrum fails to capture clear signatures of the transition, consistently exhibiting brown-noise-like behavior across regimes. In contrast, the interacting case reveals a marked change: the metallic phase displays spectral fluctuations consistent with pink noise, while the insulating phase is characterized by brown noise. These results are supported by analyses of the level spacing distribution and the level number variance. Additionally, we demonstrate that both statistics and the structure of energy eigenstates provide reliable indicators of the transition, in both interacting and non-interacting scenarios.

AI.tldr: The paper revisits the metal-insulator transition in a 1D quasiperiodic lattice with spin-1/2 particles and tunable nearest-neighbor interactions. Using the power spectrum of consecutive level spacings, the authors show that in the interacting case the metallic phase exhibits pink-noise-like spectral fluctuations while the insulating phase shows brown noise, enabling clear detection of the transition. In the non-interacting case, the power-spectrum consistently shows brown-noise-like behavior and fails to clearly capture the transition.
AI.motivation: To identify robust spectral indicators of the metal-insulator transition in quasiperiodic systems, particularly examining whether the power spectrum of energy level spacings can distinguish metallic and insulating phases, which has not been clearly established in the non-interacting setting.
AI.method: The authors compute the power-spectrum (squared modulus of the Fourier transform of consecutive level spacings) for a 1D lattice with on-site quasiperiodic potential and spin-1/2 particles with tunable nearest-neighbor interactions. They compare non-interacting and interacting cases, and corroborate findings with level spacing distribution and level number variance analyses, alongside energy eigenstate structure.
AI.result: In the non-interacting case, the power-spectrum consistently shows brown-noise-like behavior and fails to capture clear signatures of the transition. In the interacting case, the metallic phase exhibits pink-noise spectral fluctuations while the insulating phase shows brown noise, providing a clear marker of the transition. These results are supported by conventional statistics (level spacing distribution and level number variance), and both statistics and eigenstate structure reliably indicate the transition in both scenarios.
AI.conclusion: The power-spectrum of level spacings is an effective diagnostic tool for the metal-insulator transition in interacting quasiperiodic systems, where it distinguishes pink-noise (metallic) from brown-noise (insulating) fluctuations. Additional statistical and eigenstate-structure analyses serve as reliable indicators for both interacting and non-interacting cases.

title: Entropic signatures of the single-impurity Kondo state
