summary: The Kondo singlet---a many-body state formed by entanglement between a localized spin and the Fermi sea---has been studied extensively through its transport signatures in quantum dots. Here we report a thermodynamic measurement of the entropy suppression associated with the formation of the Kondo singlet, using temperature-dependent charge sensing and a Maxwell relation to track the suppression of spin entropy as the first electron is added to a strongly-coupled GaAs quantum dot. Plotting $dN/dT$ against the simultaneously measured occupation $N$ reveals an asymmetric lineshape with its peak shifted to $N>1/2$---a hallmark of Kondo screening---that weakens with increasing temperature and is qualitatively reproduced by numerical renormalization group (NRG) calculations, with a small but persistent offset to lower occupation relative to the theory. An independent measurement of conductance versus occupation on the same device provides a test of these quantities through the mixed-valence crossover and matches NRG within experimental uncertainty.

AI.tldr: This paper reports the first direct thermodynamic measurement of entropy suppression associated with Kondo singlet formation in a strongly-coupled GaAs quantum dot, using temperature-dependent charge sensing and a Maxwell relation. The dN/dT vs. N plot shows an asymmetric lineshape with peak shifted to N>1/2—a hallmark of Kondo screening—that weakens with temperature and matches NRG calculations, with conductance measurements independently confirming the results.
AI.motivation: While Kondo singlets have been extensively studied through transport signatures in quantum dots, there has been no direct thermodynamic measurement of the entropy suppression associated with their formation. The authors aim to provide a thermodynamic probe of this many-body state.
AI.method: The authors use temperature-dependent charge sensing on a strongly-coupled GaAs quantum dot and apply a Maxwell relation to track spin entropy suppression as the first electron is added. They plot dN/dT against occupation N, and compare results with NRG calculations. They also perform independent conductance versus occupation measurements on the same device to cross-validate the results through the mixed-valence crossover.
AI.result: The dN/dT vs. N plot reveals an asymmetric lineshape with peak shifted to N>1/2, a hallmark of Kondo screening, that weakens with increasing temperature. The results are qualitatively reproduced by NRG calculations, though with a small persistent offset to lower occupation relative to theory. Independent conductance measurements match NRG within experimental uncertainty.
AI.conclusion: This work provides the first direct thermodynamic measurement of the entropy suppression accompanying Kondo singlet formation, complementing the traditional transport-based studies. The agreement with NRG validates the interpretation, while the small occupation offset suggests minor discrepancies between experiment and theory that warrant further investigation.

title: Flat-band formation and chiral superconductivity in driven topological insulators
comment: The main text contains 6 pages and 2 figures
summary: We demonstrate that circularly polarized light can be used to Floquet-engineer nearly flat or Mexican-hat like electronic bands on the surface of three-dimensional topological insulators (3D TIs), which under suitable conditions, can support topological superconductivity via purely repulsive Coulomb interactions. The driving acts not merely by gapping out the Dirac cone on the surface of the 3D TI, but can be used to diminish, and even flip in sign, the intrinsic curvature of the surface state dispersion away from the Dirac point. Using parameters for canonical 3D TIs, we find that the flat band limit is attained for reasonable electric fields and the bands realized by changing the strength of the driving field have a similar energetic and spatial profile to those obtained in rhombohedral graphene under varying displacement field, where the case for superconductivity with purely repulsive interactions has recently been made. We find that, with the aid of appropriately placed screening metallic gate, one can obtain $T_c \sim 7 $K in this setup while avoiding Wigner crystallization for low electron densities in the range of $10^{11}-10^{12}/\text{cm}^2$.

AI.tldr: Circularly polarized light can Floquet-engineer nearly flat or Mexican-hat electronic bands on 3D topological insulator surfaces, enabling topological superconductivity via purely repulsive Coulomb interactions, with predicted T_c ~7K using screening metallic gates.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate that circularly polarized light can not only gap the Dirac cone on 3D TI surfaces but also flatten the surface state dispersion, creating conditions for superconductivity driven by purely repulsive interactions—offering a tunable, light-driven alternative to existing flat-band platforms like rhombohedral graphene.
AI.method: Floquet engineering of 3D TI surface states using circularly polarized light; tuning the driving field strength to diminish or reverse the intrinsic curvature of surface-state dispersion, transforming the Dirac cone into nearly flat or Mexican-hat bands; incorporating screening metallic gates to suppress Wigner crystallization; using parameters for canonical 3D TIs for realistic estimates.
AI.result: Flat-band limit is achievable with reasonable electric fields; the field-tunable bands exhibit energetic and spatial profiles analogous to rhombohedral graphene under varying displacement field; with screening gates, T_c ~7 K is obtained for electron densities in the 10^11–10^12/cm^2 range while avoiding Wigner crystallization.
AI.conclusion: Circularly polarized light provides a powerful, tunable knob to engineer flat-band physics on 3D TI surfaces, enabling repulsive-interaction-driven topological superconductivity at experimentally accessible temperatures—establishing a new, light-controlled platform for strongly correlated topological phenomena.

title: PASS: Perturbation augmented space group structure sampling for transferable Fe-O machine learning interatomic potential
summary: Accurate atomistic modelling of iron (Fe) oxidation requires a reliable interatomic potential, which necessitates an extensive and representative first-principles dataset for training the interatomic potential. However, Fe-oxygen (O) system is known for its structural and magnetic complexity, rendering the generation of high-quality dataset challenging. In this work, we propose the Perturbation Augmented Space group structure Sampling (PASS) method to generate extensive and representative dataset consisting of small-cell structures with less than 10 atoms. We present a systematic approach to developing a first of its kind transferable machine learning interatomic potential (MLIP) for Fe-O system based on the atomic cluster expansion (ACE) framework. We thoroughly validate the accuracy and capability of the ACE MLIP across both pure Fe and Fe-O systems through bulk, surface, and interface properties. We showcase the formation of FeO-like structure in large-scale Fe oxidation simulation using the ACE MLIP. This work demonstrates that the PASS method yields an accurate and transferable MLIP which is capable of capturing the reactive complexity of oxide growth while remaining computationally practical for extended systems.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Perturbation Augmented Space group structure Sampling (PASS) method to generate a diverse first-principles dataset of small-cell Fe-O structures (less than 10 atoms), which is used to train a transferable machine learning interatomic potential (MLIP) based on the atomic cluster expansion (ACE) framework. The ACE MLIP is validated across bulk, surface, and interface properties of pure Fe and Fe-O systems, and successfully simulates large-scale Fe oxidation with FeO-like structure formation.
AI.motivation: Fe-O systems exhibit structural and magnetic complexity that makes generating high-quality first-principles datasets for interatomic potential training challenging. A reliable and transferable potential is essential for accurate atomistic modelling of Fe oxidation, but existing approaches struggle to produce representative datasets and accurate potentials for this system.
AI.method: The PASS method generates extensive and representative datasets of small-cell structures (less than 10 atoms) via perturbation augmented space group sampling. These datasets train a machine learning interatomic potential built on the atomic cluster expansion (ACE) framework, providing a systematic pathway for developing a transferable MLIP for the Fe-O system.
AI.result: The ACE MLIP is thoroughly validated against bulk, surface, and interface properties for both pure Fe and Fe-O systems. Large-scale Fe oxidation simulations using the ACE MLIP successfully demonstrate the formation of FeO-like structures, confirming the potential's capability to capture reactive oxide growth complexity.
AI.conclusion: The PASS method produces an accurate and transferable MLIP that captures the reactive complexity of Fe oxide growth while maintaining computational practicality for extended systems, representing a first-of-its-kind transferable machine learning interatomic potential for the Fe-O system.

title: Machine Learning for Designing Undesignable Metal-Organic Frameworks
summary: Many crucial processes are too complex for computational modeling, requiring experimentation to identify promising materials. Here, a methodology for material design is presented, while photocatalysis is presented as a specific case-study. Metal-Organic Frameworks (MOFs) are a subset of highly promising porous nanomaterials, used in a variety of unmodellable applications. Reinforcement learning generated 60,000 novel MOFs optimized for CO/H20 selectivity. A predictor funnel system was created, iteratively removing low-scoring MOFs to 10,986 potential candidates, improving computational efficiency by 276%. While trained Crystal Graph Convolutional Neural Network (CGCNN) models predicted features for creating a fitness function incorporating stability, catalytic ability, material cost, sustainability, and adsorption while allowing the inclusion of application specific design criterion. This designed function provides a computational method to model photocatalytic performance- and filtered down to two promising MOFs which each pass a myriad of synthesis criteria, first a Cr-based MOF with photocatalyst score 230% higher than the control. Second, a Zn-based MOF outperforms the best control across all relevant metrics, demonstrating robustness against variable fitness functions. This work designed 20 materials, each 125% better than the control for this application. Furthermore, analysis revealed insightful design patterns, such as the significant influence of metal cluster N262 on catalytic performance, providing a method for future work to narrow the chemical space. By incorporating industrially applicable features such as cost or stability of the material, this work successfully designs industrially promising materials in otherwise unmodellable processes such as drug delivery, while paving a method for multi-objective optimization incorporating 260% more features than prior work.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a reinforcement learning and multi-objective optimization methodology for designing Metal-Organic Frameworks (MOFs) for photocatalysis. The pipeline generated 60,000 novel MOFs, used a predictor funnel system to improve computational efficiency by 276%, and applied trained CGCNN models with a fitness function incorporating stability, catalytic ability, cost, sustainability, and adsorption. The approach yielded two promising MOFs (Cr-based and Zn-based) with photocatalyst scores up to 230% higher than controls, and designed 20 materials each 125% better than the control, while revealing key design patterns such as the influence of metal cluster N262 on catalytic performance.
AI.motivation: Many critical processes are too complex for computational modeling, requiring experimental trial-and-error to identify promising materials. The authors aim to provide a computational methodology for material design in such unmodellable applications, using photocatalysis with MOFs as a case study.
AI.method: Reinforcement learning generated 60,000 novel MOFs optimized for CO/H2O selectivity. A predictor funnel system iteratively removed low-scoring MOFs down to 10,986 candidates, improving computational efficiency by 276%. Trained Crystal Graph Convolutional Neural Network (CGCNN) models predicted features, and a fitness function was constructed incorporating stability, catalytic ability, material cost, sustainability, and adsorption, while allowing application-specific design criteria.
AI.result: The pipeline filtered down to two promising MOFs: a Cr-based MOF with a photocatalyst score 230% higher than the control, and a Zn-based MOF that outperformed the best control across all relevant metrics, demonstrating robustness against variable fitness functions. Overall, 20 materials were designed, each 125% better than the control. Analysis revealed design patterns, notably the significant influence of metal cluster N262 on catalytic performance.
AI.conclusion: By incorporating industrially applicable features such as cost and stability, this work successfully designs industrially promising materials in otherwise unmodellable processes, and paves the way for multi-objective optimization incorporating 260% more features than prior work.

title: Nonclassical condensation pathways revealed by the multivariable theory of nucleation
summary: We extend classical nucleation theory (CNT) by explicitly incorporating the multidimensional nature of nucleation and the coupled roles of kinetics and thermodynamics. Specifically, we treat the cluster density as an independent variable, within both sharp-interface and diffuse-interface descriptions. The kinetics are governed by dynamical density functional theory. Applied to liquid condensation in the Lennard-Jones system, our two-variable (size--density) and three-variable (size--interface width--density) models reveal nonclassical nucleation mechanism. At low supersaturation, both models recover the classical picture, in which clusters nucleate and grow at the equilibrium liquid density. As supersaturation increases, a nonclassical behavior emerges: the critical cluster density decreases, and the nucleation pathway involves concomitant evolution in cluster size, density, and, within the diffuse-interface description, interfacial width. Our model with diffuse interface reveals a rapid increase in interfacial diffuseness at high supersaturation. Near the spinodal limit, both models predict the critical cluster with diverging sizes, densities approaching that of the metastable initial phase, and vanishing work of formation, which provides a smooth connection between nucleation and spinodal decomposition. Comparison with molecular dynamics simulations demonstrates that both models substantially outperform CNT. However, the weak non-monotonic dependence of the critical cluster density observed at very low supersaturation is captured only by diffuse-interface models. Overall, our findings indicate that CNT should be applied only in the low-supersaturation regime, and our work provides a robust foundation for its refinement beyond this limit.

AI.tldr: The authors extend classical nucleation theory by incorporating cluster density as an independent variable within both sharp- and diffuse-interface descriptions, governed by dynamical density functional theory. Applied to Lennard-Jones condensation, the two- and three-variable models reveal nonclassical nucleation mechanisms at higher supersaturation, recover classical behavior at low supersaturation, and smoothly connect to spinodal decomposition near the spinodal limit, outperforming CNT against molecular dynamics simulations.
AI.motivation: Classical nucleation theory (CNT) is insufficient for describing nucleation at moderate to high supersaturation where clusters deviate from bulk equilibrium properties. The authors aim to capture the multidimensional and coupled kinetic-thermodynamic nature of nucleation by treating cluster density as an independent variable.
AI.method: Two theoretical models are developed: a two-variable (size-density) sharp-interface model and a three-variable (size-interface width-density) diffuse-interface model. Cluster kinetics are governed by dynamical density functional theory. The models are applied to liquid condensation in the Lennard-Jones system and benchmarked against molecular dynamics simulations.
AI.result: At low supersaturation, both models reproduce the classical nucleation picture. At higher supersaturation, critical cluster density decreases and nucleation proceeds via coupled evolution of size, density, and interfacial width. Near the spinodal limit, both models predict diverging critical cluster sizes, densities approaching the metastable phase, and vanishing work of formation, smoothly bridging nucleation and spinodal decomposition. Both models substantially outperform CNT, though only the diffuse-interface model captures the weak non-monotonic density dependence at very low supersaturation.
AI.conclusion: CNT is valid only in the low-supersaturation regime. The proposed extensions provide a robust theoretical foundation for refining nucleation theory beyond this limit by explicitly accounting for the multidimensional nature of the nucleation pathway.

title: Cavity Tuning of the CDW--Superconductivity Interplay in a Kagome Metal
summary: Kagome metals host competing electronic orders, including charge-density-wave (CDW) order and superconductivity, shaped by intertwined lattice, electronic-correlation, and kagome-geometric effects. Here, using quantum electrodynamical density functional theory, we identify an equilibrium cavity route for reshaping this balance in the kagome metal CsV$_3$Sb$_5$. An out-of-plane polarized single-mode cavity selectively softens CDW-related phonons, counteracting pressure-induced hardening and extending the CDW instability toward higher pressures. In the high-pressure regime where the CDW instability is otherwise suppressed, cavity coupling redistributes Eliashberg spectral weight toward lower frequencies, enhances the total electron--phonon coupling (EPC), and increases the EPC-based Allen--Dynes estimate of $T_c$. This response originates from a charge-density redistribution induced by the out-of-plane photon mode, which modifies lattice restoring forces and drives the phonon and EPC renormalization. These results establish cavity quantum electrodynamics as a viable equilibrium route for tuning intertwined charge order, lattice dynamics, and superconductivity in kagome materials.

AI.tldr: Using quantum electrodynamical density functional theory, the authors show that an out-of-plane polarized single-mode cavity can selectively soften CDW-related phonons in the kagome metal CsV3Sb5, extending the CDW instability toward higher pressures while simultaneously enhancing electron-phonon coupling and the Allen-Dynes estimate of Tc in the high-pressure regime where CDW is suppressed. The effect arises from photon-induced charge-density redistribution that alters lattice restoring forces.
AI.motivation: Kagome metals exhibit intertwined electronic orders (CDW and superconductivity) shaped by lattice, correlation, and geometric effects. The authors seek a new equilibrium route to control this competition—specifically, whether cavity quantum electrodynamics can be used to reshape the balance between CDW order and superconductivity in CsV3Sb5.
AI.method: The study employs quantum electrodynamical density functional theory (QED-DFT) to simulate the kagome metal CsV3Sb5 coupled to an out-of-plane polarized single-mode optical cavity. The analysis tracks CDW phonon softening/hardening as a function of pressure, examines Eliashberg spectral function redistribution, computes total electron-phonon coupling, and estimates Tc via the Allen-Dynes formula.
AI.result: The out-of-plane cavity mode selectively softens CDW-related phonons, counteracting pressure-induced hardening and extending CDW instability to higher pressures. In the high-pressure regime where CDW is suppressed, cavity coupling redistributes Eliashberg spectral weight to lower frequencies, enhances total EPC, and increases the Allen-Dynes Tc estimate. These effects stem from charge-density redistribution induced by the photon mode modifying lattice restoring forces.
AI.conclusion: Cavity quantum electrodynamics provides a viable equilibrium route for tuning intertwined charge order, lattice dynamics, and superconductivity in kagome materials, offering a new knob to control competing electronic orders.

title: Non-reciprocity drives a Brownian dimer out of equilibrium
summary: We consider the minimal model of a two dimensional Brownian dimer consisting of two overdamped monomers, trapped in an isotropic harmonic potential and mutually coupled by a non-reciprocal harmonic spring that violates Newton's action-reaction principle. We have shown that the non-reciprocal interaction alone can drive the system far from equilibrium, in the absence of any external time dependent drive and being in contact with a single thermal bath. The exact steady state probability distribution and current are explicitly calculated for the zero-rest-length limit of the spring, which eventually maps our model to another non-equilibrium phenomenon, called Brownian gyration. For a spring with finite rest length, these quantities are calculated numerically.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes a minimal model of a two-dimensional Brownian dimer—two overdamped monomers trapped in an isotropic harmonic potential and coupled by a non-reciprocal harmonic spring—and shows that the non-reciprocal interaction alone drives the system far from equilibrium without external time-dependent drives or multiple baths. Exact steady-state probability distribution and current are derived for the zero-rest-length limit (mapping to Brownian gyration), while finite rest-length cases are treated numerically.
AI.motivation: Non-reciprocal interactions, which violate Newton's action-reaction principle, are known to drive systems out of equilibrium. The authors aim to demonstrate that such interactions alone—without external time-dependent driving or multiple thermal baths—can sustain a far-from-equilibrium steady state in a minimal model, providing exact analytical results for a canonical Brownian dimer system.
AI.method: The model consists of two overdamped Brownian monomers in a 2D isotropic harmonic trap, mutually coupled by a non-reciprocal harmonic spring. The exact steady-state probability distribution and probability current are computed analytically in the zero-rest-length limit, which maps to Brownian gyration. For a spring with finite rest length, the same quantities are obtained numerically.
AI.result: The non-reciprocal spring interaction alone is sufficient to drive the system far from equilibrium, even in the presence of only a single thermal bath and no external time-dependent drive. Exact steady-state distributions and currents are obtained analytically for the zero-rest-length case (recovering Brownian gyration), and numerically for finite rest lengths.
AI.conclusion: Non-reciprocal interactions constitute a sufficient mechanism to maintain a non-equilibrium steady state in a minimal Brownian dimer model, connecting to the broader phenomenon of Brownian gyration and offering a tractable framework for studying non-equilibrium dynamics driven solely by interaction asymmetry.

title: Third-order nonlinear transport in a percolative two-dimensional superconductor
summary: Percolative superconductivity frequently arises in two-dimensional van der Waals materials due to reduced dimensionality, enhanced quantum fluctuations, and complex electron-phonon interactions, providing a unique platform where normal electrons coexist with Cooper pairs. We report the observation of substantial third-order nonlinear transport in a trilayer $1T^\prime$-MoTe$_2$ superconductor within its percolative transition regime. The third-harmonic longitudinal voltage ($V_{\|}^{3ω}$) exhibits a clear cubic dependence on excitation current below a threshold, with both its magnitude and nonlinear coefficient strongly correlated with the superconducting state. This nonlinear response is semiquantitatively captured by the superconducting fluctuation within the time-dependent Ginzburg-Landau theory, where nonlinear transport arises due to fluctuating Cooper pairs. Our results demonstrate that third-order nonlinear transport serves as a sensitive probe of superconducting transitions in percolative systems and establish a foundation for exploring higher-order transport phenomena in strongly correlated systems.

AI.tldr: The paper reports the observation of substantial third-order nonlinear transport in a trilayer 1T'-MoTe2 superconductor within its percolative transition regime. The third-harmonic longitudinal voltage exhibits cubic dependence on excitation current, semiquantitatively captured by time-dependent Ginzburg-Landau theory via fluctuating Cooper pairs, demonstrating that third-order nonlinear transport is a sensitive probe of percolative superconducting transitions.
AI.motivation: Percolative superconductivity in two-dimensional van der Waals materials offers a unique platform where normal electrons coexist with Cooper pairs, but conventional linear transport measurements may not sensitively capture the percolative superconducting transition dynamics. The authors seek a more sensitive probe—specifically, third-order nonlinear transport—to investigate the superconducting transition in this regime.
AI.method: The authors performed third-order nonlinear transport measurements on a trilayer 1T'-MoTe2 superconductor within its percolative transition regime. They measured the third-harmonic longitudinal voltage (V||^3ω) as a function of excitation current, and analyzed its cubic dependence below a threshold. The results were compared semiquantitatively with the time-dependent Ginzburg-Landau (TDGL) theory, where nonlinear transport arises from superconducting fluctuations of Cooper pairs.
AI.result: The third-harmonic longitudinal voltage exhibits a clear cubic dependence on excitation current below a threshold. Both the magnitude of the nonlinear response and the nonlinear coefficient are strongly correlated with the superconducting state. The nonlinear transport behavior is semiquantitatively captured by the TDGL theory incorporating superconducting fluctuations.
AI.conclusion: Third-order nonlinear transport serves as a sensitive probe of superconducting transitions in percolative systems. This work establishes a foundation for exploring higher-order transport phenomena in strongly correlated systems.

title: Excited state optimization for strongly correlated quantum defects using ensemble variational Monte Carlo
summary: Using the recently introduced ensemble variational Monte Carlo (VMC), we study optimized wave functions for strongly correlated point defects, including nitrogen-vacancy and silicon-vacancy centers in diamond and substitutional iron and chromium impurities in aluminum nitride. We study the effects of fully optimized determinant expansion parameters, orbitals, and Jastrow correlation factors on these systems. We find that orbitals from the hybrid functional PBE0 are much better (have lower objective functional) than semilocal PBE, which results in changes in the excitation energies up to 0.5 eV. Further improvements can be made by directly optimizing the objective functional, resulting in changes in excitation energies up to 0.2 eV. The most important parameter varies from defect to defect, reinforcing the necessity of optimizing all parameters to obtain accurate excited states in strongly correlated defects.

AI.tldr: This paper uses ensemble variational Monte Carlo (VMC) to study optimized wave functions for strongly correlated point defects, including NV and SiV centers in diamond and Fe/Cr impurities in AlN. It finds that PBE0 hybrid-functional orbitals outperform semilocal PBE orbitals (changing excitation energies by up to 0.5 eV), and further direct optimization of the objective functional yields additional changes up to 0.2 eV, with the most critical variational parameter varying from defect to defect.
AI.motivation: Strongly correlated point defects in semiconductors are challenging to describe accurately with standard methods. The authors aim to determine which variational parameters (determinant expansion, orbitals, Jastrow factors) most significantly affect the accuracy of excited states, and whether ensemble VMC can systematically optimize these wave functions.
AI.method: The authors apply the recently introduced ensemble variational Monte Carlo approach to optimize fully determinant-expanded, orbital-optimized, and Jastrow-corrected wave functions for several point defects. They compare starting orbitals from PBE (semilocal) versus PBE0 (hybrid) functionals, and then directly optimize all parameters against the ensemble objective functional.
AI.result: PBE0 starting orbitals yield substantially lower objective functionals than PBE orbitals, producing excitation energy shifts up to 0.5 eV. Direct optimization of the objective functional provides further improvements, changing excitation energies by up to 0.2 eV. The relative importance of different variational parameters varies across defects, indicating that no single parameter dominates universally.
AI.conclusion: Accurate excited states in strongly correlated point defects require simultaneous optimization of all wave function parameters—determinant expansions, orbitals, and Jastrow factors—since their relative importance is system-dependent. Ensemble VMC provides a robust framework for achieving this.

title: Graph Neural Network Force Fields for Spin Dynamics in Metallic Magnets
summary: Metallic magnets exhibit complex spin dynamics governed by electronically generated interactions. Predictive simulations of such dynamics typically require repeated solutions of an underlying electronic problem throughout the time evolution, creating a major computational bottleneck. Here we introduce a graph neural network (GNN) magnetic force-field framework that learns the effective magnetic energy functional governing itinerant spin dynamics directly from electronic calculations. Conceptually analogous to machine-learned interatomic potentials, the proposed framework enables efficient evaluation of spin torques while capturing the nonlinear and spatially extended interactions generated by itinerant electrons. We benchmark the method on representative metallic magnetic systems exhibiting collinear, noncollinear, and noncoplanar magnetic order. The learned force fields accurately reproduce electronically generated spin torques and yield nonequilibrium spin dynamics in excellent agreement with direct electronic simulations. Our results establish graph neural networks as a powerful framework for machine-learned magnetic force fields, providing a pathway toward predictive large-scale simulations of nonequilibrium magnetism across multiple length and time scales.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a graph neural network (GNN) magnetic force-field framework that learns the effective magnetic energy functional for itinerant spin dynamics directly from electronic calculations, enabling efficient spin-torque evaluation and large-scale nonequilibrium magnetic simulations without repeated electronic problem solving.
AI.motivation: Predictive simulations of metallic magnet spin dynamics are computationally prohibitive because they require repeatedly solving the underlying electronic problem at every time step throughout the evolution. This creates a major computational bottleneck that limits the achievable length and time scales of such simulations.
AI.method: The authors propose a GNN-based magnetic force-field framework that learns the effective magnetic energy functional governing itinerant spin dynamics from electronic structure calculations. Analogous to machine-learned interatomic potentials, the GNN captures nonlinear and spatially extended spin interactions generated by itinerant electrons and enables efficient evaluation of spin torques.
AI.result: The method is benchmarked on representative metallic magnetic systems exhibiting collinear, noncollinear, and noncoplanar magnetic order. The learned force fields accurately reproduce electronically generated spin torques, and nonequilibrium spin dynamics match direct electronic simulations with excellent agreement.
AI.conclusion: The results establish graph neural networks as a powerful framework for machine-learned magnetic force fields, offering a pathway toward predictive large-scale simulations of nonequilibrium magnetism across multiple length and time scales.

title: Evolution of the Irradiation Induced Defect Landscape through Dislocation Vacancy Loop Interactions in Tungsten
summary: Structural materials for fusion reactors undergo neutron irradiation, generating defect populations that govern their mechanical response through irradiation hardening. Physically based mesoscale constitutive models require accurate descriptions of dislocation defect interactions and, critically, how both defect morphology and obstacle strength evolve during plastic deformation as the irradiation-induced defect landscape changes. Vacancy loops provide an ideal prototype for addressing this problem because they are among the most prevalent irradiation-induced defects in tungsten, yet their interaction mechanisms with dislocations and subsequent evolution remain poorly understood. Molecular dynamics simulations are used to systematically investigate interactions between edge dislocations and vacancy loops in tungsten by varying loop size, crystallographic orientation, and dislocation loop intersection geometry. Parallel loops exhibit strong geometry dependent behaviour, undergoing complete annihilation, transformation into weaker remnant defects, or defect transport depending on the interaction geometry. In contrast, inclined loops interact through Burgers vector reactions that form sessile <100> dislocation segments, producing substantially higher pinning strengths with little sensitivity to the intersection position. Finally, a framework is demonstrated for translating atomistically determined obstacle strengths into constitutive parameters, such as irradiation hardening, for mesoscale models. The mechanistic understanding developed here provides the physical basis for future mesoscale constitutive laws that explicitly account for the evolution of irradiation-induced defect populations and the resulting changes in dislocation-defect interaction mechanisms and obstacle strength, thereby improving predictive capability beyond calibrated conditions.

AI.tldr: This study uses molecular dynamics simulations to systematically investigate edge dislocation-vacancy loop interactions in tungsten, revealing that parallel loops exhibit geometry-dependent behaviors (annihilation, transformation, or transport) while inclined loops form sessile <100> segments with stronger pinning. A framework is demonstrated for translating atomistic obstacle strengths into mesoscale constitutive parameters for irradiation hardening models.
AI.motivation: Physically based mesoscale constitutive models for fusion reactor materials require accurate descriptions of dislocation-defect interactions, including how defect morphology and obstacle strength evolve during plastic deformation. Vacancy loops are among the most prevalent irradiation-induced defects in tungsten, yet their interaction mechanisms with dislocations and subsequent evolution are poorly understood.
AI.method: Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations systematically investigating edge dislocation interactions with vacancy loops in tungsten, varying loop size, crystallographic orientation, and dislocation-loop intersection geometry. Additionally, a framework is demonstrated for translating atomistically determined obstacle strengths into mesoscale constitutive parameters.
AI.result: Parallel loops show strong geometry-dependent behavior: complete annihilation, transformation into weaker remnant defects, or defect transport. Inclined loops interact via Burgers vector reactions forming sessile <100> dislocation segments, yielding substantially higher pinning strengths with little sensitivity to intersection position.
AI.conclusion: Mechanistic understanding from MD simulations provides the physical basis for future mesoscale constitutive laws that explicitly account for the evolution of irradiation-induced defect populations and resulting changes in dislocation-defect interaction mechanisms and obstacle strength, improving predictive capability beyond calibrated conditions.

title: Wavelength-Resolved Photoinduced Spin Polarization in a Broad Optical Range for a Porphyrin-Quinone System
summary: Photochemically induced dynamic nuclear polarization (photo-CIDNP) in liquid-state donor-acceptor systems is typically studied at a limited number of excitation wavelengths, leaving its spectral dependence incompletely characterized. Understanding the wavelength dependence of photo-CIDNP is important both for elucidating the underlying spin-chemical mechanisms and for optimizing hyperpolarization strategies in chemically and biologically relevant molecular systems. Here, we investigate wavelength-resolved photo-CIDNP in a tetraphenylporphyrin-1,4-benzoquinone donor-acceptor system over the 350-800 nm spectral range. Photon-flux-normalized CIDNP amplitudes were measured using both a tunable laser system and a broadband xenon lamp equipped with interchangeable 10 nm interference filters. The CIDNP response exhibits a non-monotonic dependence on excitation wavelength. Pronounced hyperpolarization is observed near 350 nm and in the 500-550 nm region, whereas excitation within the strongly absorbing 400-450 nm range results in a substantially reduced CIDNP response. Comparison with the UV-Vis absorption spectrum demonstrates that photo-CIDNP efficiency is not governed solely by optical absorption and reflects wavelength-dependent photophysical processes. After normalization to the excitation photon flux, lamp- and laser-based measurements yield consistent CIDNP results, validating broadband filtered excitation as a reliable and experimentally accessible approach for wavelength-resolved photo-CIDNP studies. These results establish excitation wavelength as an independent control parameter for liquid-state photo-CIDNP and provide a framework for systematic investigations of wavelength-dependent spin hyperpolarization.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates wavelength-resolved photo-CIDNP in a tetraphenylporphyrin-1,4-benzoquinone donor-acceptor system across 350-800 nm, revealing a non-monotonic CIDNP response that does not simply track optical absorption. Notably strong hyperpolarization occurs near 350 nm and 500-550 nm, while the strongly absorbing 400-450 nm region gives reduced CIDNP. The study validates broadband filtered xenon lamp excitation as a reliable alternative to tunable lasers after photon-flux normalization.
AI.motivation: Photo-CIDNP is typically studied at only a few excitation wavelengths, leaving its spectral dependence poorly characterized. Understanding wavelength dependence is crucial for elucidating underlying spin-chemical mechanisms and for optimizing hyperpolarization strategies in chemically and biologically relevant systems.
AI.method: Wavelength-resolved photo-CIDNP was measured in a tetraphenylporphyrin-1,4-benzoquinone system over 350-800 nm using both a tunable laser system and a broadband xenon lamp with interchangeable 10 nm interference filters. CIDNP amplitudes were normalized to photon flux and compared with the UV-Vis absorption spectrum.
AI.result: The CIDNP response is non-monotonic with wavelength: strong hyperpolarization appears near 350 nm and in the 500-550 nm region, while the strongly absorbing 400-450 nm range shows substantially reduced CIDNP. Photo-CIDNP efficiency does not correlate solely with optical absorption, indicating wavelength-dependent photophysical processes. After photon-flux normalization, lamp-and laser-based measurements give consistent results.
AI.conclusion: Excitation wavelength is established as an independent control parameter for liquid-state photo-CIDNP. Broadband filtered excitation is validated as a reliable, experimentally accessible approach for wavelength-resolved photo-CIDNP studies, providing a framework for systematic investigation of wavelength-dependent spin hyperpolarization.

title: Symmetry, Sound, and the Quest for Chiral Superconductors
summary: The confirmation of a bulk, topological superconductor is a central goal of modern quantum materials research. Despite decades of searching, no confirmed examples yet exist. A primary difficulty is that most experimental signatures of topological superconductivity are ambiguous and indirect. I review efforts to narrow the search for a chiral topological superconductor using measurements of elastic moduli. In principle, these experiments can provide unambiguous thermodynamic evidence for multi-component superconductivity---a pre-requisite for chiral superconductivity in 2D and quasi-2D materials. Despite the potential strength of this program, the results are still negative. I provide a pedagogical introduction to multi-component order parameters, chiral topological superconductivity, and how superconducting order parameters couple to strain. I discuss ongoing efforts in heavy fermion, iron pnictide, and Kagome superconductors, and suggest routes for speeding up the search process, as well as other experimental tools that should be developed for the pursuit of this goal.

AI.tldr: This paper reviews the search for chiral topological superconductors using elastic moduli measurements, arguing that while these experiments can provide unambiguous thermodynamic evidence for multi-component superconductivity—a prerequisite for chiral superconductivity—the results remain negative across heavy fermion, iron pnictide, and Kagome superconductors.
AI.motivation: Despite decades of searching, no bulk topological superconductor has been confirmed. Most experimental signatures of topological superconductivity are ambiguous and indirect, so the field needs a more reliable experimental pathway to narrow the search.
AI.method: The paper provides a pedagogical review combining: (1) an introduction to multi-component order parameters and chiral topological superconductivity, (2) an explanation of how superconducting order parameters couple to strain, and (3) a survey of elastic moduli measurements applied to heavy fermion, iron pnictide, and Kagome superconductors.
AI.result: Elastic moduli measurements can in principle provide unambiguous thermodynamic evidence for multi-component superconductivity, a necessary condition for chiral superconductivity in 2D and quasi-2D materials; however, all results from this program to date remain negative.
AI.conclusion: The author suggests routes to accelerate the search process and identifies additional experimental tools that should be developed to pursue the goal of confirming a chiral topological superconductor.

title: Ensemble theory of thermodiffusion
summary: Heat flow sustained by a temperature difference generates a gradient of matter as observed, for example, in atomistic simulations of hard-core gases. We use path-ensemble theory to represent the coupled thermal and diffusive transport by dynamics on a graph. Calibrated from a single equilibrium simulation, this model accurately predicts nonequilibrium mass distribution in a hard-core gas across a wide range of applied temperature gradients. It also enables estimation of transport properties, such as the Soret coefficient, using analytical expressions.

AI.tldr: The paper uses path-ensemble theory to model coupled thermal and diffusive transport as graph dynamics, calibrated from a single equilibrium simulation, accurately predicting nonequilibrium mass distributions in hard-core gases across a wide range of temperature gradients, and enabling analytical estimation of transport properties like the Soret coefficient.

The goal is to develop a predictive theoretical framework that can accurately model these coupled thermal-diffusive transport phenomena without requiring extensive nonequilibrium simulations.

The model is calibrated using data from a single equilibrium simulation and then applied to predict nonequilibrium behavior. title: Significant ordinary Nernst effect contribution to spin-orbit torque harmonic Hall measurements in metallic structures
summary: The harmonic Hall measurements are commonly used to quantify the spin-orbit torque in ferromagnet/normal metal bilayers. The contribution from ordinary Nernst effect to the second harmonic voltages is usually assumed to be negligible and omitted in the data analysis. We show that in Cr/Co bilayers the ordinary Nernst effect cannot be neglected and can lead to largely exaggerated values of spin-orbit torque efficiency. Conducting additional experiments, we estimate the Nernst coefficient of Cr and find it comparable to the values reported for other metals. Consequently, the ordinary Nernst effect should be carefully considered when employing the harmonic Hall technique to quantify spin-orbit torque in metals, while the results of some previous works might need to be re-examined.

AI.tldr: This paper reveals that the ordinary Nernst effect, typically neglected in harmonic Hall measurements, can significantly exaggerate spin-orbit torque efficiency values in Cr/Co bilayers. The Nernst coefficient of Cr is comparable to other metals, suggesting previous harmonic Hall results in metals may need re-examination.
AI.motivation: The harmonic Hall technique is widely used to quantify spin-orbit torque in ferromagnet/normal metal bilayers. The ordinary Nernst effect contribution to second harmonic voltages is commonly assumed negligible and omitted, but this assumption may be invalid and could lead to erroneous spin-orbit torque values.
AI.method: The authors conduct harmonic Hall measurements on Cr/Co bilayers and perform additional control experiments to isolate and estimate the ordinary Nernst contribution. They quantify the Nernst coefficient of Cr by separating it from the spin-orbit torque signal.
AI.result: The ordinary Nernst effect in Cr/Co bilayers is significant and cannot be neglected. The estimated Nernst coefficient of Cr is comparable to values reported for other metals, and ignoring this effect leads to largely exaggerated spin-orbit torque efficiency values.
AI.conclusion: The ordinary Nernst effect should be carefully considered in harmonic Hall analysis of spin-orbit torque in metals. The findings imply that some previously reported spin-orbit torque efficiencies may be overestimated and warrant re-examination.

title: Universality of Energy-Space Entanglement in Quantum Impurity Models
summary: Entanglement entropy (EE) is commonly studied using real-space bipartitions. We show that, in quantum impurity models, an energy-space bipartition, equivalent to the momentum-space bipartition of the bath, can display universal behavior. Motivated by poor man's scaling, we logarithmically discretize the bath and partition it into high- and low-energy sectors. For models with Fermi-liquid fixed points, including the Anderson model and fully screened or underscreened Kondo models, the low-energy EE flows to constants independent of model parameters. These constants are integer multiples of $\ln 2$ plus corrections that depend only on the logarithmic discretization parameter $Λ$. We show that scale invariance of the fixed-point wavefunction in energy space maps to effective translation invariance along a one-dimensional chain, allowing the fixed points to be classified by one-dimensional topological band theory. With low-energy chiral symmetry, each $\ln 2$ contribution originates from a topological edge mode. We also study transitions between distinct Fermi-liquid fixed points using the local-singlet--Kondo-singlet transition in a two-orbital Anderson model driven by an inter-orbital antiferromagnetic coupling. The local-singlet phase has an effectively decoupled impurity and nearly vanishing EE, whereas the Kondo-singlet phase has finite EE larger than $\ln 2$ per spin and orbital. When chiral symmetry holds at low energies, this distinction corresponds to a topological transition of the effective bath chain. At the non-Fermi-liquid critical point, the EE develops an unstable plateau. Its $Λ$ dependence resembles that of the overscreened two-channel Kondo model, supporting universality within the same non-Fermi-liquid universality class.

For Fermi-liquid fixed points, the low-energy EE flows to constants that are integer multiples of ln 2 plus Λ-dependent corrections, classifiable via one-dimensional topological band theory with each ln 2 arising from a topological edge mode. Transitions between Fermi-liquid fixed points (e.g., local-singlet to Kondo-singlet) correspond to topological transitions, and the non-Fermi-liquid critical point exhibits universal EE behavior similar to the overscreened two-channel Kondo model.
AI.motivation: Traditional studies of entanglement entropy (EE) rely on real-space bipartitions. The authors aim to show that energy-space bipartitions—equivalent to momentum-space bipartitions of the bath—can also exhibit universal behavior in quantum impurity models, providing a new perspective on classifying quantum impurity fixed points.
AI.method: The authors logarithmically discretize the bath (motivated by poor man's scaling) and partition it into high- and low-energy sectors. They analyze the resulting EE using Fermi-liquid fixed points of Anderson and Kondo models, relate scale invariance of the fixed-point wavefunction in energy space to effective translation invariance along a one-dimensional chain, and classify fixed points using topological band theory with chiral symmetry. They also study the two-orbital Anderson model across the local-singlet to Kondo-singlet transition and the non-Fermi-liquid critical point.

Each ln 2 originates from a topological edge mode under low-energy chiral symmetry. The local-singlet phase has nearly vanishing EE while the Kondo-singlet phase has finite EE exceeding ln 2 per spin and orbital, corresponding to a topological transition. At the non-Fermi-liquid critical point, the EE develops an unstable plateau with Λ dependence resembling the overscreened two-channel Kondo model.
AI.conclusion: Energy-space bipartitions provide a new universal framework for studying quantum impurity models, connecting entanglement entropy to topological classification. This supports universality within a non-Fermi-liquid universality class and offers a topological characterization of quantum impurity fixed points and transitions between them.

title: PEDOT:PSS-Coated Magnetoelastic Sensors for Highly Sensitive Wireless Humidity Sensing
summary: Magnetoelastic (ME) resonators provide an attractive platform for passive and wireless sensing, particularly for monitoring relative humidity (RH) in sealed or hard-to-access environments. In this work, we introduce ME humidity sensors functionalized with poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene) sulfonate (PEDOT), marking the first application of this conductive polymer in ME-based humidity sensing. PEDOT films were deposited onto Metglas resonators via a simple drop-casting process, producing uniform and mechanically stable coatings. Comprehensive structural and morphological characterization by SEM, EDX, Raman spectroscopy, AFM/KPFM, and XRD confirmed the structural integrity of the polymer and revealed humidity-induced swelling of the PSS-rich domains, accompanied by enhanced polymer-chain mobility and an increase in the lamellar spacing from 23.5 Å to 24.2 Å at 95% RH. These structural changes directly affected the dynamic response of the resonators, leading to a systematic resonance-frequency downshift driven by the combined effects of water adsorption, mass loading, and viscoelastic damping. The optimized device achieved a sensitivity of 155 Hz/% RH in the 20 - 70% RH range, outperforming previously reported ME humidity sensors, while exhibiting a resolution better than 0.1% RH together with excellent response and recovery times. These results establish PEDOT as a highly effective functional coating for magnetoelastic humidity sensors and demonstrate a simple, low-cost, wireless sensing platform with high sensitivity and strong potential for practical environmental and industrial monitoring applications.

The sensor achieves a sensitivity of 155 Hz/% RH in the 20-70% RH range with resolution better than 0.1% RH, demonstrating a low-cost, wireless, passive sensing platform that outperforms previously reported ME humidity sensors.

Humidity-induced changes (PSS swelling, chain mobility increase, lamellar spacing expansion from 23.5 to 24.2 Å at 95% RH) were correlated with the resonator dynamic response, where water adsorption, mass loading, and viscoelastic damping drive resonance-frequency downshifts.

AI.conclusion: PEDOT is established as a highly effective functional coating for magnetoelastic humidity sensing, providing a simple, low-cost, wireless sensing platform with high sensitivity and strong potential for practical environmental and industrial monitoring applications.

title: Quantum Computing Enabled ab initio Molecular Dynamics Simulations
comment: 45 pages, 7 figures. Supporting Information included as an ancillary file
summary: We demonstrate a quantum-classical workflow for ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) in which quantum measurements from a chemistry-inspired LUCJ ansatz are post-processed using Sample-based Quantum Diagonalization (SQD) to recover determinant subspaces and deliver energies and analytical nuclear gradients for dynamics. As an exact benchmark, we use full configuration interaction (FCI) in the STO-3G basis, enabling a direct assessment of the accuracy of SQD. In gas-phase benchmarks, SQD reproduces FCI energies and gradients to within 1 kcal mol$^{-1}$ of the FCI reference and yields stable AIMD trajectories. In explicit-solvent QM/MM simulations, SQD retains this agreement, matching FCI energy fluctuations and RMS gradient profiles and reproducing solute-solvent structure as quantified by radial distribution functions. Overall, these benchmarks establish LUCJ+SQD as a practical route for integrating current quantum hardware into QM/MM molecular dynamics and provide an early demonstration of condensed-phase QM/MM dynamics driven by a quantum electronic-structure engine.

Benchmarked against full configuration interaction (FCI) in STO-3G, the method achieves energies and gradients within 1 kcal mol⁻¹ of FCI in gas phase, and reproduces FCI-level accuracy in explicit-solvent QM/MM simulations, establishing LUCJ+SQD as a practical route for integrating quantum hardware into condensed-phase molecular dynamics.

AI.method: The workflow uses a quantum measurement-driven approach where a chemistry-inspired LUCJ (Low-rank Unitary Coupled Cluster with Jastrow) ansatz is measured on quantum hardware, and the resulting samples are post-processed via Sample-based Quantum Diagonalization (SQD) to recover important determinant subspaces. Energies and analytical nuclear gradients are computed from this recovered subspace and used to drive molecular dynamics trajectories, both in the gas phase and in explicit-solvent QM/MM settings.

In explicit-solvent QM/MM simulations, SQD maintains this accuracy, matching FCI energy fluctuations and RMS gradient profiles while reproducing solute-solvent structure as quantified by radial distribution functions.
AI.conclusion: The LUCJ+SQD combination is established as a practical and accurate approach for integrating current quantum hardware into QM/MM molecular dynamics, providing an early demonstration of condensed-phase quantum-driven molecular dynamics and indicating a viable path for quantum electronic-structure engines in realistic simulation environments.

title: Mpemba effect in a chemomechanical model of the Kinesin molecular motor
summary: The Mpemba effect, wherein a system prepared farther from equilibrium relaxes faster than one initially closer to equilibrium, has been extensively investigated in a wide range of physical systems. In contrast, its role in biologically relevant non-equilibrium processes remains largely unexplored. Here, we investigate anomalous relaxation in the six-state chemomechanical network model of the Kinesin molecular motor under both equilibrium and non-equilibrium conditions. We first establish the existence of the Mpemba effect in chemical equilibrium and show that many of its qualitative features can be understood from the underlying free-energy landscape. We then examine the effects of mechanical and chemical driving, showing that breaking detailed balance primarily reshapes the Mpemba phase diagram without qualitatively altering the relaxation phenomenology over the physically relevant parameter regime. Finally, we demonstrate that the relaxation of the motor velocity also mirrors the anomalous relaxation of the underlying stochastic dynamics, thereby identifying an experimentally accessible signature of the Mpemba effect. Our results establish molecular motors as a promising baseline for studying anomalous relaxation in living systems and suggest a broader framework for exploring the Mpemba effect in non-equilibrium biochemical networks.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the Mpemba effect (anomalous relaxation where systems farther from equilibrium relax faster) in the six-state chemomechanical network model of the Kinesin molecular motor, demonstrating that this effect exists at chemical equilibrium, is reshaped but not qualitatively altered by mechanical and chemical driving, and is experimentally accessible through motor velocity relaxation.
AI.motivation: While the Mpemba effect has been extensively studied in physical systems, its role in biologically relevant non-equilibrium processes remains largely unexplored. The authors aim to fill this gap by investigating anomalous relaxation in molecular motors, which are fundamental to biological function.
AI.method: The authors analyze the six-state chemomechanical network model of the Kinesin molecular motor. They first study the existence of the Mpemba effect under chemical equilibrium conditions, interpreting qualitative features via the free-energy landscape. They then examine the effects of mechanical and chemical driving that break detailed balance, analyzing how the Mpemba phase diagram is reshaped. Finally, they investigate whether relaxation of motor velocity mirrors the anomalous relaxation of the underlying stochastic dynamics.

Breaking detailed balance via mechanical and chemical driving primarily reshapes the Mpemba phase diagram without qualitatively altering relaxation phenomenology in the physically relevant regime. The relaxation of motor velocity also mirrors the anomalous relaxation, providing an experimentally accessible signature.

title: Scalar-spin-chirality-driven fractional Chern insulator on a kagome lattice
summary: Fractional Chern insulators (FCIs) are the lattice analogs of the fractional quantum Hall states, emerging even without an external magnetic field. In this work, we demonstrate the emergence of the FCI states in a kagome magnet with a noncoplanar magnetic order that induces a finite scalar spin chirality. By incorporating in our model both electron-electron interactions and the effect of band dispersion, we find that stronger interactions relative to the band dispersion stabilize the FCI state over a broader range of scalar spin chirality. We characterize the emergent FCI state by calculating overlap with representative states, identifying the ground-state degeneracy and the finite energy gap in the thermodynamic limit, and tracking the spectral flow under multiple flux-quantum insertions. Our results suggest that kagome magnets with scalar spin chirality can be promising platforms for realizing FCIs.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates that fractional Chern insulator (FCI) states emerge in kagome magnets with noncoplanar magnetic order that induces scalar spin chirality, even without an external magnetic field. Stronger electron-electron interactions relative to band dispersion stabilize the FCI over a broader chirality range, and kagome magnets are proposed as promising FCI platforms.
AI.motivation: To identify and characterize a realistic material platform where fractional Chern insulator states can emerge without an external magnetic field, by leveraging the effective magnetic fields generated by noncoplanar magnetic orders with scalar spin chirality in kagome lattices.
AI.method: The authors construct a model incorporating electron-electron interactions and band dispersion effects in a kagome magnet with noncoplanar magnetic order. They characterize the emergent FCI state via overlap calculations with representative states, ground-state degeneracy and finite energy-gap analysis in the thermodynamic limit, and spectral flow tracking under multiple flux-quantum insertions.
AI.result: Stronger interactions relative to band dispersion stabilize the FCI state over a broader range of scalar spin chirality. The FCI state is confirmed through ground-state degeneracy, finite energy gap in the thermodynamic limit, and characteristic spectral flow under flux insertion.
AI.conclusion: Kagome magnets with scalar spin chirality represent promising platforms for realizing fractional Chern insulator states without external magnetic fields.

title: Iterative minimization in reduced density matrix functional theory for periodic systems
summary: Reduced density matrix functional theory (RDMFT) offers a route beyond Kohn-Sham density functional theory for strongly correlated systems, yet practical calculations for periodic solids are still out of reach. We formulate RDMFT for extended systems in a basis-independent way and present a planewave implementation using iterative minimization for periodic solids, evaluating nonlocal exchange-correlation functionals through the existing adaptive compressed exchange machinery. Natural occupations are optimized under N-representability constraints with a spectral projected gradient (SPG) method or an first-order explicit-by-implicit (EBI) map, while natural orbitals are updated by Riemannian optimization on the complex Stiefel manifolds. Benchmarks on typical systems of \ce{H2}, silicon, and sodium with the Hartree-Fock functional show that SPG reproduces converged hybrid references, whereas EBI can stall when occupations approach $0$ or $1$. With the power and Müller functionals, SPG yields lower energies and more stable convergence than EBI. Applications to fractionally charged \ce{LiH}, dissociating \ce{H2} and \ce{N2} molecules, and equation of state of silicon show that the algorithm presented in this implementation is reliable and robust.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a basis-independent formulation of reduced density matrix functional theory (RDMFT) for periodic solids, with a planewave implementation using iterative minimization. Natural occupations are optimized via spectral projected gradient (SPG) or explicit-by-implicit (EBI) methods, while natural orbitals are updated via Riemannian optimization on complex Stiefel manifolds. Benchmarks on H2, silicon, and sodium show SPG reliably reproduces hybrid references and outperforms EBI, especially with power and Müller functionals. Applications to fractionally charged LiH, dissociating H2/N2, and silicon's equation of state demonstrate robustness.
AI.motivation: RDMFT provides a route beyond Kohn-Sham DFT for strongly correlated systems, but practical calculations for periodic solids remain out of reach. This work aims to bridge that gap by developing a practical planewave implementation for extended systems.

Natural occupations are optimized under N-representability constraints using either spectral projected gradient (SPG) or first-order explicit-by-implicit (EBI) methods. Natural orbitals are updated through Riemannian optimization on complex Stiefel manifolds. Nonlocal exchange-correlation functionals are evaluated via adaptive compressed exchange machinery.

With power and Müller functionals, SPG yields lower energies and more stable convergence than EBI. title: Optimization of Epitaxial Mn4N Thin Films Grown by Sputtering for Spintronic Applications
summary: Ferrimagnetic Mn4N has recently emerged as a promising rare-earth-free platform for spintronic devices due to its low magnetization, high domain wall mobility, and strong anomalous Hall response. However, the realization of thin films with robust perpendicular magnetic anisotropy (PMA) and spin-orbit torque (SOT) functionality through scalable deposition techniques remains a significant challenge. In this work, we systematically investigate the growth of Mn4N thin films by reactive magnetron sputtering and determine the conditions required to achieve high-quality films suitable for SOT applications. We demonstrate that epitaxial, single-crystalline Mn4N films with strong PMA can be obtained on MgO(100), whereas films deposited on SrTiO3(100) exhibit a textured structure. The optimized films show square-shaped hysteresis loops with high remanence, large and tunable coercivity, and a pronounced anomalous Hall effect. By combining structural, magnetic, and magnetotransport characterization with density functional theory calculations, we reveal that epitaxial strain plays a key role in tuning magnetic anisotropy, while also showing that it is not the only contributing factor. In particular, our results emphasize the importance of interfacial effects in stabilizing PMA. Finally, we demonstrate efficient current-induced magnetization switching in Mn4N/Pt bilayers, confirming strong interfacial spin transparency. These findings establish sputtered Mn4N as a promising and versatile material platform for energy-efficient spin-orbitronic devices.

AI.tldr: This work demonstrates that ferrimagnetic Mn4N thin films grown by reactive magnetron sputtering on MgO(100) achieve epitaxial, single-crystalline quality with strong perpendicular magnetic anisotropy (PMA), while films on SrTiO3(100) are textured. The authors show that both epitaxial strain and interfacial effects contribute to PMA, and demonstrate efficient current-induced magnetization switching in Mn4N/Pt bilayers, establishing sputtered Mn4N as a scalable, rare-earth-free platform for spintronic devices.
AI.motivation: Mn4N is a promising rare-earth-free ferrimagnetic material for spintronics due to low magnetization, high domain wall mobility, and strong anomalous Hall response, but achieving thin films with robust PMA and spin-orbit torque functionality via scalable deposition methods remains challenging.
AI.method: Systematic growth of Mn4N films by reactive magnetron sputtering on MgO(100) and SrTiO3(100) substrates, combined with structural, magnetic, and magnetotransport characterization and density functional theory calculations. Bilayers with Pt were fabricated to test SOT-driven magnetization switching.
AI.result: Epitaxial single-crystalline Mn4N films with strong PMA were obtained on MgO(100), while SrTiO3(100) produced textured films. Optimized films show square hysteresis loops, high remanence, large tunable coercivity, and pronounced anomalous Hall effect. DFT revealed that both epitaxial strain and interfacial effects control PMA. Efficient current-induced magnetization switching was demonstrated in Mn4N/Pt bilayers, confirming strong interfacial spin transparency.
AI.conclusion: Sputtered Mn4N is established as a promising and versatile rare-earth-free material platform for energy-efficient spin-orbitronic devices, with scalable deposition, robust PMA, and efficient SOT functionality.

title: Wavefunction-based periodic quantum chemistry
summary: High-accuracy molecular quantum chemistry offers a promising toolbox for applications to condensed-phase systems, but this field is difficult to enter due to its combination of topics from molecular quantum chemistry, solid-state physics, and numerical methods. Aiming to ease this transition, we present a comprehensive, pedagogical tutorial on periodic quantum chemistry calculations, using both mean-field and correlated theories. The subtleties of periodic Coulomb interactions are discussed in detail, focusing on the Ewald summation approach. We describe the two most popular periodic, one-electron basis functions---plane waves and periodic linear combinations of atomic orbitals---and we give formulas for all Hamiltonian integrals. Next, we explain the use of $k$-point sampling as a symmetry adaptation of supercell basis functions and the associated savings in computational costs as well as the use of density fitting and related approximations to further reduce costs. We present the working equations of a few example periodic quantum chemistry methods, including Hartree-Fock theory, perturbation theory, and coupled-cluster theory, and we discuss their finite-size errors and convergence to the physically relevant thermodynamic limit. Finally, we briefly discuss local correlation and quantum embedding theories, which are especially appropriate for periodic systems due to their lattice translational symmetries.

AI.tldr: A comprehensive pedagogical tutorial on periodic quantum chemistry calculations covering mean-field and correlated theories, with detailed discussions of Ewald summation, plane-wave and atomic-orbital basis functions, k-point sampling, density fitting, example methods (HF, perturbation theory, coupled-cluster), finite-size errors, and local correlation/quantum embedding approaches.
AI.motivation: The field of periodic (condensed-phase) quantum chemistry is difficult to enter because it combines molecular quantum chemistry, solid-state physics, and numerical methods. The authors aim to ease this transition for researchers by providing a comprehensive, pedagogical tutorial.
AI.method: The paper presents a step-by-step tutorial covering: (1) periodic Coulomb interactions via Ewald summation, (2) the two most popular one-electron basis functions (plane waves and periodic linear combinations of atomic orbitals) with formulas for all Hamiltonian integrals, (3) k-point sampling as a symmetry adaptation of supercell basis functions and cost reduction via density fitting, (4) working equations for example methods including Hartree-Fock, perturbation theory, and coupled-cluster theory, and (5) discussion of local correlation and quantum embedding theories appropriate for periodic systems with lattice translational symmetry.
AI.result: The paper provides the full working equations for several periodic quantum chemistry methods, analysis of finite-size errors and convergence to the thermodynamic limit, and highlights which methods (local correlation and quantum embedding) are particularly suited to periodic systems.
AI.conclusion: This tutorial serves as an accessible entry point for researchers wishing to apply high-accuracy molecular quantum chemistry methods to condensed-phase systems, bridging the gap between molecular and solid-state computational approaches.

title: Three-Dimensional Kardar--Parisi--Zhang Scaling in Polariton Condensates
summary: Kardar--Parisi--Zhang (KPZ) universality provides an example of macroscopic scaling generated by microscopic violation of detailed balance. While one- and two-dimensional realizations have been explored in driven condensates and growing interfaces, demonstrating KPZ scaling in three spatial dimensions remains a major challenge. Here we propose a three-dimensional exciton-polariton crystal as a platform for observation of 3D KPZ universality. Starting from a stochastic driven-dissipative Gross-Pitaevskii equation for a condensate formed in a three-dimensional photonic-crystal lower-polariton band, we eliminate the massive density and reservoir modes and obtain an effective $3+1$-dimensional KPZ equation for the condensate phase. Numerical simulations of both the KPZ equation and the full driven-dissipative polariton model show an intermediate-asymptotic regime in which the first-order coherence obeys $-\ln |\gone(0,Δt)|\propto |Δt|^{2β}$ and $-\ln |\gone(Δr,0)|\propto |Δr|^{2χ}$, with exponents consistent with the $3+1$ KPZ benchmarks $β= 0.1845$, $χ= 0.3135$. Our results identify three-dimensional polariton crystals as a controllable quantum fluid route to higher-dimensional nonequilibrium universality.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a three-dimensional exciton-polariton crystal as a platform to observe Kardar-Parisi-Zhang (KPZ) universality in 3+1 dimensions. By deriving an effective KPZ equation for the condensate phase from a stochastic driven-dissipative Gross-Pitaevskii equation, the authors show via numerical simulations that both the KPZ equation and the full polariton model exhibit intermediate-asymptotic scaling of first-order coherence consistent with 3D KPZ benchmarks (β=0.1845, χ=0.3135), establishing polariton crystals as a route to higher-dimensional nonequilibrium universality.
AI.motivation: While KPZ universality—macroscopic scaling generated by microscopic violation of detailed balance—has been experimentally explored in one and two dimensions (driven condensates, growing interfaces), demonstrating KPZ scaling in three spatial dimensions remains a major open challenge. This work aims to fill that gap by identifying a physically realizable 3D platform.
AI.method: Starting from a stochastic driven-dissipative Gross-Pitaevskii equation for a condensate in a three-dimensional photonic-crystal lower-polariton band, the authors adiabatically eliminate the massive density and reservoir modes to derive an effective 3+1-dimensional KPZ equation for the condensate phase. They then perform numerical simulations of both the KPZ equation and the full driven-dissipative polariton model, extracting exponent scaling from the first-order coherence functions.

AI.conclusion: Three-dimensional polariton crystals represent a controllable quantum-fluid platform for observing higher-dimensional nonequilibrium universality, specifically 3D KPZ scaling, which had previously remained elusive.

title: Giant nonlinear Hall effect in a Pt/ferrimagnetic insulator bilayer under Zeeman-exchange frustration
summary: Competing magnetic interactions can create metastable or unstable states and render magnetic systems highly susceptible to external perturbations. Here we show that Zeeman-exchange frustration in an Al-substituted terbium iron garnet with a compositional gradient across its thickness gives rise to a giant nonlinear Hall response in an adjacent Pt layer. Near magnetic compensation, a field-induced spin-flip transition is accompanied by unusually large higher-order odd harmonic voltages, with the third, fifth, and seventh harmonics reaching amplitudes comparable to that of the first harmonic. The field, temperature, and current dependences collectively identify Joule heating as the parametric drive of the harmonic response. Macrospin-chain simulations further show that current-induced thermal modulation periodically switches the interfacial Fe magnetization between exchange- and Zeeman-dominated states and reproduces the observed harmonic signals. These results demonstrate how frustration can convert a weak thermal perturbation into a large nonlinear electrical response, providing a route to nonlinear magnetotransport in compensated ferrimagnets.

AI.tldr: In an Al-substituted terbium iron garnet with a compositional thickness gradient, Zeeman-exchange frustration near magnetic compensation produces a giant nonlinear Hall response in an adjacent Pt layer. A field-induced spin-flip transition generates large odd harmonic voltages (third, fifth, seventh) comparable to the first harmonic. Joule heating acts as the parametric drive, and macrospin-chain simulations show current-induced thermal modulation periodically switches interfacial Fe magnetization between exchange- and Zeeman-dominated states, reproducing observed harmonics.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate how magnetic frustration near compensation can convert a weak thermal perturbation into a large nonlinear electrical response, offering a new route to nonlinear magnetotransport in compensated ferrimagnets.
AI.method: Experimental harmonic Hall measurements on Pt adjacent to an Al-substituted TbIG film with a compositional gradient, combined with field/temperature/current dependence analysis and macrospin-chain simulations to model the current-induced thermal modulation of interfacial magnetization.
AI.result: Observation of unusually large odd harmonic voltages (third through seventh) near the field-induced spin-flip transition, with amplitudes comparable to the first harmonic. Joule heating is identified as the parametric drive, and macrospin-chain simulations reproduce the observed harmonic signals.
AI.conclusion: Zeeman-exchange frustration in compensated ferrimagnets can amplify thermal perturbations into giant nonlinear electrical responses, establishing a pathway for nonlinear magnetotransport in ferrimagnetic heterostructures.

title: Trion Excitations in Twisted Bilayer Graphene: A Quantum Monte Carlo Study
comment: 8 pages, 4 figures in the main text, 5 pages, 1 figure in the Supplemental Material
summary: Determining the nature of charge carriers is a fundamental goal in the study of strongly correlated electron systems. Here, we employ the continuous-field momentum-space quantum Monte Carlo method to reveal exotic "Dirac trion" excitations in the finite-temperature normal state of twisted bilayer graphene. While the ground state is a symmetry-breaking insulator with gapped ($\sim$ 20 meV) electron-like excitations, we show that a small temperature ($\sim$ 3 meV), well below the interaction scale, drives the system into a strongly fluctuating symmetric normal state. We demonstrate that this normal state hosts gapless excitations consisting of three-particle bound states, two electrons and one hole, that are exactly orthogonal to the higher-energy electrons at the zero-momentum gapless point. These Dirac trions have the remarkable property of being arbitrarily light despite being composed of heavy constituents, and their spectra can be easily tuned by varying the twist angle and interlayer hopping strength. Our unbiased quantum many-body computation sheds light on the Dirac trions in a projected correlated flat-band setting and opens the door for further investigation of many-body excitations in strongly correlated topological bands beyond Landau levels.

AI.tldr: Using continuous-field momentum-space quantum Monte Carlo, this paper reveals "Dirac trion" excitations in twisted bilayer graphene's finite-temperature normal state—gapless three-particle bound states (two electrons, one hole) that are orthogonal to higher-energy electrons and arbitrarily light despite heavy constituents.
AI.motivation: Determining the nature of charge carriers is a fundamental goal in studying strongly correlated electron systems, motivating a search for exotic many-body excitations in twisted bilayer graphene beyond conventional Landau-level physics.
