AI.method: The authors employ continuous-field momentum-space quantum Monte Carlo to compute the finite-temperature normal state of twisted bilayer graphene, analyzing excitation spectra and bound-state structures.
AI.result: A small temperature (~3 meV), well below the interaction scale, drives the symmetry-breaking gapped insulator into a strongly fluctuating symmetric normal state hosting gapless Dirac trion excitations—three-particle bound states (2e + 1h) orthogonal to higher-energy electrons at the zero-momentum gapless point. These trions are arbitrarily light despite heavy constituents and their spectra are tunable via twist angle and interlayer hopping.
AI.conclusion: The unbiased quantum many-body computation reveals Dirac trions in a projected correlated flat-band setting, opening the door for investigating many-body excitations in strongly correlated topological bands beyond Landau levels.

title: Structure and thermodynamic stability of $β$-Ga$_2$O$_3$ surfaces
summary: We present a comprehensive first-principles investigation of all symmetrically inequivalent low-index surfaces of $β$-Ga$_2$O$_3$, examining their structural properties and thermodynamic stability across experimentally relevant growth conditions. Using density-functional theory with both semi-local (PBEsol) and hybrid (PBE0) functionals, we calculate surface free energies for the (010), (100), (001), ($\bar{2}01$), (110), (111), and ($11\bar{1}$) orientations, including the effects of harmonic vibrational contributions and varying oxygen chemical potentials. We demonstrate that the energetic ordering remains consistent across computational approaches and that the vibrational contributions remain below 0.2 J/m$^2$ up to temperatures of 1000 K. A coordination-based model that correlates surface stability with the density of under-coordinated atoms reveals that under-coordinated oxygen atoms and tetrahedral Ga sites substantially destabilize surfaces, while exposed under-coordinated octahedral Ga atoms serve as indicators of surface stability. Our thermodynamic analysis shows that stoichiometric terminations dominate over nearly the entire range of chemical potentials relevant for $β$-Ga$_2$O$_3$ stability, while non-stoichiometric terminations emerge only under extreme reducing or oxidizing conditions. Notably, we predict the formation of stable Ga-rich terminations resembling Ga adlayers for the (100) and ($\bar{2}01$) surfaces under highly reducing conditions.

AI.tldr: A first-principles DFT study of all low-index β-Ga₂O₃ surfaces, examining structural stability and thermodynamic properties across growth conditions using PBEsol and PBE0 functionals, revealing that stoichiometric terminations dominate and that under-coordinated atoms govern surface stability.
AI.motivation: To provide a comprehensive understanding of the surface thermodynamics of β-Ga₂O₃, a material of significant technological interest, across its various low-index facets and growth conditions—an essential foundation for crystal growth and device processing.
AI.method: Density-functional theory with semi-local (PBEsol) and hybrid (PBE0) functionals; calculation of surface free energies for seven low-index orientations (010, 100, 001, 2̄01, 110, 111, 11̄1) including harmonic vibrational contributions and varying oxygen chemical potentials; a coordination-based stability model based on under-coordinated atom density.
AI.result: Energetic ordering is consistent across functionals; vibrational contributions remain below 0.2 J/m² up to 1000 K; under-coordinated oxygen and tetrahedral Ga destabilize surfaces while under-coordinated octahedral Ga indicate stability; stoichiometric terminations dominate across nearly all relevant chemical potentials; Ga-rich adlayer-like terminations predicted on (100) and (2̄01) under highly reducing conditions.
AI.conclusion: The surface thermodynamics of β-Ga₂O₃ are robustly characterized, with stoichiometric terminations prevailing under realistic growth conditions and stable Ga-rich reconstructions predicted under reducing environments, providing guidance for growth and processing of this semiconductor.

title: Finite-size effects and interaction-driven crossovers in quarter-filled attractive Hubbard model: Exact diagonalization, DMRG and machine-learning analysis
summary: We investigate the quarter-filled attractive Hubbard model on finite-width cylindrical lattices using exact diagonalization (ED), density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) and unsupervised machine-learning-based techniques. Analysis of the ground-state energetics, local observables and correlation functions reveals a continuous interaction-driven crossover from weakly correlated fermions to a regime dominated by tightly bound singlet pairs. This crossover originates from the competition between kinetic-energy-driven fermionic itinerancy and interaction-driven onsite pair formation and exhibits behavior consistent with the BCS--BEC crossover in the thermodynamic limit. Hole-binding-energy calculations provide direct energetic evidence for pair formation: the two-hole binding energy remains negative throughout the attractive regime whereas three-hole binding emerges only at sufficiently strong attraction and exhibits pronounced finite-size dependence. To obtain an unbiased characterization of the correlation landscape, we apply principal component analysis (PCA) and uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) to the real-space correlation matrices. PCA reveals a systematic redistribution of correlation variance whereas UMAP identifies a clear separation between weak- and strong-pairing regimes. Both machine-learning-based approaches independently identify the same crossover region inferred from conventional observables while providing an order-parameter-independent characterization of the underlying reorganization of many-body correlations. Finite-size scaling analyses of the pairing structure factor and the leading PCA variance ratio demonstrate that these signatures remain robust with increasing system size.

AI.tldr: The paper studies the quarter-filled attractive Hubbard model on finite-width cylindrical lattices using exact diagonalization, DMRG, and unsupervised machine learning (PCA and UMAP). It reveals a continuous BCS-BEC crossover from weakly correlated fermions to tightly bound singlet pairs, confirmed by energetic (hole-binding), correlation-based, and machine-learning-identified signatures that remain robust under finite-size scaling.
AI.motivation: To obtain an unbiased, order-parameter-independent characterization of the BCS-BEC crossover in the attractive Hubbard model on finite-width cylinders, and to identify whether machine-learning approaches can independently recover the crossover region inferred from conventional observables.
AI.method: Combines exact diagonalization (ED), density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG), and unsupervised machine-learning techniques (principal component analysis, PCA, and uniform manifold approximation and projection, UMAP). Ground-state energetics, local observables, correlation functions, and hole-binding energies are computed; PCA and UMAP are applied to real-space correlation matrices, supplemented by finite-size scaling analyses of the pairing structure factor and leading PCA variance ratio.
AI.result: A continuous interaction-driven crossover from weakly correlated fermions to tightly bound singlet pairs is found, consistent with BCS-BEC crossover. The two-hole binding energy stays negative in the attractive regime while three-hole binding emerges only at strong attraction with pronounced finite-size effects. PCA shows systematic redistribution of correlation variance, and UMAP clearly separates weak- and strong-pairing regimes; both methods independently identify the same crossover region. Finite-size scaling confirms the robustness of these signatures with increasing system size.
AI.conclusion: Unsupervised machine-learning analysis provides an order-parameter-independent identification of the BCS-BEC crossover that agrees with conventional observables, establishing the crossover's robustness with system size and demonstrating the utility of data-driven approaches for characterizing many-body correlation reorganization.

title: From Exponential to Gaussian Tails: Fractal Wavefront Scaling and the $κ$-Weibull Distribution at Phase Transitions
summary: The paper examines the features of critical evolution in an active medium modeled by a cellular automaton. The system evolves according to stochastic rules, exhibiting two qualitatively distinct dynamical regimes: one of fading activity and another of all-filling activity waves. Each regime is characterized by its own fractal dimension and fluctuation statistics, both of which are analyzed in detail. Within the critical interval, the system displays a nontrivial fractal dimension and a fluctuation distribution that bridges the two regimes. This bridging behavior arises because, in the critical interval, the dynamics are governed by avalanches.

AI.tldr: This paper studies critical evolution in a cellular automaton model of an active medium, identifying two distinct dynamical regimes (fading activity and all-filling activity waves) characterized by different fractal dimensions and fluctuation statistics. At the critical interval, the system exhibits a nontrivial fractal dimension and bridging fluctuation distributions, governed by avalanche dynamics.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to understand critical phenomena in active media by analyzing the dynamical regimes and their statistical properties, particularly how criticality emerges and is characterized in a stochastic cellular automaton system.
AI.method: The system is modeled as a cellular automaton evolving under stochastic rules. The authors characterize two qualitatively distinct dynamical regimes—fading activity and all-filling activity waves—and analyze their fractal dimensions and fluctuation statistics. The critical interval is analyzed separately to reveal its bridging properties.
AI.result: The two regimes each possess their own distinct fractal dimension and fluctuation statistics. In the critical interval, the system displays a nontrivial fractal dimension and a fluctuation distribution that bridges the two regimes, with dynamics governed by avalanches.
AI.conclusion: Critical evolution in this active medium is governed by avalanche dynamics, producing a bridging behavior between fading activity and all-filling activity wave regimes, characterized by a nontrivial fractal dimension and intermediate fluctuation statistics.

title: Hyperchaos in a Magnetic Nanodisk Driven by Ferromagnetic Resonance
summary: We investigate the chaotic dynamics driven in the nonlinear regime of ferromagnetic resonance of an out-of-plane magnetized nanodisk in detail. By combining extensive micromagnetic simulations with time-series analysis across the control parameter space, we map the topological transitions from stable periodic orbits to strange attractors and quantify the dynamical complexity. Despite the simplicity of our nanoscale system, we evidence that it can exhibit hyperchaotic dynamics with up to three positive Lyapunov exponents in vast regions of the control plane accessible to experimental studies. Using a mode projection technique, we unveil that the generated complexity is related to the number of quantized spin-wave modes participating in the dynamics. Our findings establish magnon-spintronic nanodevices as versatile entropy sources for unconventional processing of information.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates chaotic dynamics in nonlinear ferromagnetic resonance of an out-of-plane magnetized nanodisk, using micromagnetic simulations and time-series analysis to map transitions from stable periodic orbits to strange attractors. They demonstrate hyperchaotic dynamics with up to three positive Lyapunov exponents and link the complexity to the number of participating quantized spin-wave modes, establishing magnon-spintronic nanodevices as entropy sources for unconventional computing.
AI.motivation: To understand the chaotic dynamics achievable in a simple nanoscale magnetic system and to establish spintronic nanodevices as viable entropy sources for unconventional information processing, requiring detailed mapping of dynamical complexity across parameter space.
AI.method: Combining extensive micromagnetic simulations with nonlinear time-series analysis across control parameter space, including Lyapunov exponent computation to quantify dynamical complexity and characterize hyperchaos, plus a mode projection technique to identify participating quantized spin-wave modes.
AI.result: The nanodisk exhibits hyperchaotic dynamics with up to three positive Lyapunov exponents in vast regions of the experimentally accessible control plane. The generated complexity is directly related to the number of quantized spin-wave modes participating in the dynamics, evidencing that even simple nanoscale systems can produce rich chaotic behavior.
AI.conclusion: Magnon-spintronic nanodevices can serve as versatile entropy sources for unconventional processing of information, with their chaotic and hyperchaotic dynamics being experimentally accessible and tunable through the number of active spin-wave modes.

title: Decoding the Micromagnetic Hamiltonian from Magnetic Fingerprints
summary: Extracting intrinsic magnetic Hamiltonians directly from magnetometry is challenging due to the high dimensionality of the parameter space and the degeneracy induced by ensemble averaging. Here, we introduce a collection of deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to extract the full phenomenological micromagnetic Hamiltonian directly from the magnetic fingerprints encoded within First-Order Reversal Curves (FORCs). We validate this approach via closed-loop verification, re-creating the input magnetometry for both simulated and experimental FORCs. To mitigate false positives, we deploy an `Alice--Bob' parallel network that quantifies prediction uncertainty based on solely the information in FORCs without any additional ground-truth knowledge. This framework provides a robust, machine-learning-assisted approach to unravel the underlying spin behaviors in complex magnetic systems

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a deep CNN framework to extract full phenomenological micromagnetic Hamiltonians directly from First-Order Reversal Curves (FORCs), validated via closed-loop verification and paired with an 'Alice-Bob' parallel network to quantify prediction uncertainty without ground-truth data.
AI.motivation: Extracting intrinsic magnetic Hamiltonians from magnetometry is challenging due to the high dimensionality of the parameter space and degeneracy induced by ensemble averaging, necessitating a more robust approach to unravel underlying spin behaviors.
AI.method: A collection of deep convolutional neural networks processes magnetic fingerprints encoded in FORCs to extract the full phenomenological micromagnetic Hamiltonian. An 'Alice-Bob' parallel network quantifies prediction uncertainty using only information in FORCs without ground-truth knowledge.
AI.result: The approach was validated via closed-loop verification, successfully re-creating input magnetometry for both simulated and experimental FORCs, while mitigating false positives through uncertainty quantification.
AI.conclusion: This framework provides a robust, machine-learning-assisted approach to unravel underlying spin behaviors in complex magnetic systems by directly extracting magnetic Hamiltonians from magnetometry data.

title: Anomalous metal and superconducting phases in rhombohedral graphene
summary: Two-dimensional superconductivity is now well established in graphene-based systems, with many such realizations showing evidence for unconventional pairing. Yet in several of the gate-tuned phases that otherwise exhibit clear signatures of superconductivity, the resistance does not vanish as temperature is lowered, instead saturating at a finite value. Here we report a systematic study of this behavior in rhombohedral graphene on a WSe$_2$ substrate, finding regions of gate space with zero-resistance superconductivity alongside others with finite saturation resistance. At zero magnetic field, these regions appear as isolated pockets in gate space that otherwise exhibit strikingly similar phenomenology, including abrupt transitions to the normal state as temperature, perpendicular magnetic field, and current are raised above critical values. A small in-plane field expands and merges these pockets without qualitatively altering their behavior, producing a sharp boundary at millikelvin base temperature between states of zero or finite resistance. The finite-resistance state reproduces key phenomenology associated with the anomalous metal, a state that has been observed in thin-film superconductors for decades but lacks an accepted theoretical explanation. The tunability and reproducibility of ultra-clean rhombohedral graphene place strong constraints on extrinsic explanations and provide a new platform for understanding this behavior.

AI.tldr: This paper reports a systematic study of finite saturation resistance in superconducting phases of rhombohedral graphene on WSe2, identifying isolated pockets in gate space with zero-resistance superconductivity alongside those with finite saturation resistance. The finite-resistance state reproduces key phenomenology of the "anomalous metal" state observed in thin-film superconductors, and the ultra-clean tunable platform places strong constraints on extrinsic explanations.
AI.motivation: In graphene-based superconductors, several gate-tuned phases show clear superconducting signatures but resistance does not fully vanish, saturating at a finite value as temperature is lowered. This behavior lacks an accepted theoretical explanation and its origin is poorly understood, motivating a systematic investigation.
AI.method: Systematic transport study of rhombohedral graphene on a WSe2 substrate, probing gate-tuned phases at zero magnetic field and under small in-plane fields. Resistance was measured as a function of temperature, perpendicular magnetic field, and current to map out regions of zero-resistance versus finite-saturation-resistance superconductivity in gate space.
AI.result: The gate space contains isolated pockets exhibiting either zero-resistance superconductivity or finite saturation resistance, with otherwise strikingly similar phenomenology: abrupt transitions to the normal state with increasing temperature, perpendicular field, or current. A small in-plane field expands and merges these pockets while preserving their behavior, producing a sharp boundary at millikelvin temperatures between zero and finite resistance states. The finite-resistance state reproduces hallmark features of the anomalous metal.
AI.conclusion: The finite saturation resistance in rhombohedral graphene closely resembles the anomalous metal state seen in thin-film superconductors. The exceptional tunability and reproducibility of ultra-clean rhombohedral graphene rule out many extrinsic explanations and establish it as a new platform for understanding this long-standing phenomenon.

title: Interacting Quantum Symmetric Exclusion Process
comment: 5 pages + End Matter and Supplemental Material; 2 figures
summary: We introduce and solve the Interacting Quantum Symmetric Exclusion Process (IQSEP), a family of models describing the stochastic quantum hopping of charged particles along the edges of a lattice, with hopping amplitudes that depend on the occupations of neighbouring sites. In the absence of interactions, they reduce to the standard quantum simple symmetric exclusion process, exhibiting coherent diffusive transport. For interactions of order one, they capture incoherent diffusive transport and its fluctuations, characterized by density-dependent diffusivity and mobility, making contact with the macroscopic fluctuation theory. By rescaling the interaction strength appropriately with the lattice mesh, we define a mesoscopic scaling regime that retains a finite coherence length in the continuous thermodynamic limit. This regime interpolates between coherent behavior at small length scales and incoherent behavior at large scales. The resulting scaling theory accounts for fluctuations of quantum coherences in interacting diffusive systems, going beyond the scope of standard fluctuating hydrodynamics.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces IQSEP, a family of models for stochastic quantum hopping of charged particles with occupation-dependent hopping amplitudes, interpolating between coherent and incoherent diffusive transport, and defines a mesoscopic scaling regime that retains a finite coherence length in the thermodynamic limit, extending fluctuating hydrodynamics to account for quantum coherence fluctuations.
AI.motivation: To develop a framework that captures both coherent and incoherent quantum transport in interacting diffusive systems, bridging the gap between standard quantum exclusion processes (coherent) and macroscopic fluctuation theory (incoherent), while accounting for fluctuations of quantum coherences beyond standard fluctuating hydrodynamics.
AI.method: The authors define IQSEP models where hopping amplitudes depend on neighboring site occupations, analyze the non-interacting limit recovering the quantum simple symmetric exclusion process, study order-one interactions connected to macroscopic fluctuation theory, and introduce a mesoscopic rescaling of interaction strength with lattice mesh to retain finite coherence length in the thermodynamic limit.
AI.result: The IQSEP family interpolates between coherent (small-scale) and incoherent (large-scale) diffusive behavior through a mesoscopic scaling regime, producing a scaling theory that describes density-dependent diffusivity, mobility, and fluctuations of quantum coherences in interacting diffusive systems.
AI.conclusion: IQSEP extends the scope of standard fluctuating hydrodynamics by providing a scaling framework that retains quantum coherence effects at small scales while recovering incoherent diffusive transport at large scales, unifying coherent and incoherent quantum transport descriptions.

title: Probing the Potential Profile of Twisted Bilayer Graphene via Fabry-Pérot Interference
summary: We use Fabry-Pérot interference to probe the internal potential profile of large-angle twisted bilayer graphene. We trace anomalous resistance oscillations in the nominally unipolar regime to a hidden cavity formed by unintentional local doping in our device. By analyzing zero-field interference patterns, we determine the location and size of this inhomogeneity. Magnetotransport measurements support the model, distinguishing local cavity modes from global resonances through their different magnetic dependence. Simulations using our extracted profile reproduce the experimental features. Our results highlight interference spectroscopy as a simple, non-invasive probe for identifying local defects and internal potential barriers in ballistic devices.

AI.tldr: The paper uses Fabry-Pérot interference to probe the internal potential profile of large-angle twisted bilayer graphene, identifying a hidden cavity caused by unintentional local doping. Through zero-field interference patterns and magnetotransport, the authors locate and size this inhomogeneity, distinguishing local cavity modes from global resonances, and validate their model with simulations.
AI.motivation: To understand and identify unintended local potential inhomogeneities in ballistic twisted bilayer graphene devices, which can obscure intrinsic transport properties even in nominally clean unipolar regimes.
AI.method: Fabry-Pérot interference spectroscopy at zero magnetic field to map internal potential profile; magnetotransport measurements to differentiate local cavity modes from global resonances via their distinct magnetic field dependence; profile-extraction and numerical simulations to reproduce experimental features.
AI.result: The authors trace anomalous resistance oscillations to a hidden cavity formed by unintentional local doping, determine its location and size from interference patterns, and successfully reproduce experimental observations with simulations using the extracted potential profile.
AI.conclusion: Interference spectroscopy is a simple, non-invasive tool for identifying local defects and internal potential barriers in ballistic devices, offering a pathway to characterize hidden inhomogeneities without direct imaging.

title: Orbital-Selective Mott Transition and Correlation-Amplified Charge Ordering in the Altermagnet CsCr$_2$S$_2$O
summary: Altermagnet CsCr$_2$S$_2$O undergoes a Verwey-type metal-to-insulator transition (MIT) driven by lattice distortion and a stripe charge order on the Cr sublattice, reminiscent of the physics in Fe$_3$O$_4$. However, atomic distortions occur exclusively at the ligand sites rather than the Cr sites. What drives such a pronounced charge imbalance between Cr sites thus remains a mystery. Utilizing DFT+DMFT calculations, we identify an orbital-selective Mott transition, which leaves the correlated metallic $d_{yz}$ orbital governing the low-energy physics. We demonstrate that S-site distortions trigger an initial, tiny charge asymmetry between Cr sites via Cr-$d_{yz}$ and S-$p$ orbital hybridization. Crucially, this asymmetry is significantly amplified by dynamical electronic correlations, resulting in a large discrepancy in both the charge and electron correlations of the Cr-$d_{yz}$ orbital between distinct Cr sites. This further induces a substantial differentiation in local spin polarizations in the altermagnetic state, ultimately driving the MIT. In contrast, we predict that replacing S with Te weakens this correlation-amplification effect and fails to induce an MIT due to weaker electron correlations. Our findings demonstrate that many-body effects can drastically amplify ligand instabilities to reshape the electronic structure of altermagnets, highlighting that ligand engineering is of paramount importance for realizing robust metallic altermagnetism.

AI.tldr: Using DFT+DMFT, the authors show that the Verwey-type metal-to-insulator transition in altermagnet CsCr2S2O is driven by an orbital-selective Mott transition where S-site distortions create a small charge asymmetry that is dramatically amplified by dynamical electronic correlations, leading to a MIT. Replacing S with Te weakens this effect and fails to induce a MIT.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses the mystery of what drives the pronounced charge imbalance between Cr sites in CsCr2S2O, which undergoes a Verwey-type MIT with atomic distortions occurring only at ligand (S) sites rather than the Cr sites themselves.
AI.method: DFT+DMFT (density functional theory + dynamical mean-field theory) calculations to analyze the electronic structure, orbital-resolved correlations, charge imbalance, and the role of lattice distortions at S sites.
AI.result: An orbital-selective Mott transition is identified, with the correlated metallic d_yz orbital governing low-energy physics. S-site distortions trigger a tiny charge asymmetry amplified by dynamical correlations into a large discrepancy in charge and correlation strength between Cr sites, inducing differential spin polarizations and driving the MIT. Replacing S with Te weakens the correlation-amplification and fails to induce a MIT.
AI.conclusion: Many-body effects can drastically amplify ligand instabilities to reshape the electronic structure of altermagnets, highlighting the paramount importance of ligand engineering for realizing robust metallic altermagnetism.

title: Dynamics of Null and Electrostatic Blind Spots for Quantitative PFM
summary: Piezoresponse force microscopy is a cornerstone technique for probing nanoscale electromechanical phenomena, yet quantitative and in some cases qualitative interpretation remains hindered by parasitic electrostatic forces coupled through cantilever dynamics. Recent approaches aim to suppress these artifacts by operating at resonance defined null spots or electrostatic blind spots, but whether these conditions are equivalent and how they evolve under realistic measurement conditions has remained unclear. Here, combining analytical beam models, geometrically faithful finite-element simulations, and automated interferometric measurements, we show that NS and ESBS are fundamentally different operating conditions. The NS is a modal zero at contact resonance where sensitivity to all excitations vanishes, whereas the ESBS is a quasistatic position where only the distributed electrostatic response is suppressed. Automated measurements reveal that both conditions evolve with the tip sample boundary condition yet remain spatially separated under realistic experimental conditions. While beam models capture the dominant cantilever mechanics, finite-element simulations and experiment show that quantitative prediction of near tip behavior requires realistic three dimensional probe electrostatics and mechanics. These findings establish NS and ESBS as dynamic operating conditions and provide a practical framework for advancing interferometric PFM toward truly quantitative electromechanical metrology.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates that node spots (NS) and electrostatic blind spots (ESBS) in piezoresponse force microscopy are fundamentally different operating conditions—NS being a modal zero where all excitation sensitivity vanishes at contact resonance, while ESBS is a quasistatic position suppressing only distributed electrostatic response—and shows through beam models, finite-element simulations, and automated interferometric measurements that both conditions evolve with tip-sample boundary conditions yet remain spatially distinct in practice.
AI.motivation: Quantitative and qualitative interpretation in piezoresponse force microscopy is hindered by parasitic electrostatic forces coupled through cantilever dynamics. Recent approaches suppress these artifacts via resonance-defined null spots (NS) or electrostatic blind spots (ESBS), but whether these conditions are equivalent and how they evolve under realistic measurement conditions has remained unclear.
AI.method: Combines analytical beam models, geometrically faithful finite-element simulations, and automated interferometric measurements to analyze and compare NS and ESBS conditions under realistic experimental parameters.
AI.result: NS and ESBS are fundamentally different operating conditions: NS is a modal zero at contact resonance where sensitivity to all excitations vanishes, whereas ESBS is a quasistatic position suppressing only the distributed electrostatic response. Both conditions evolve with the tip-sample boundary condition but remain spatially separated. Beam models capture dominant cantilever mechanics, but finite-element simulations and experiments show quantitative near-tip behavior prediction requires realistic 3D probe electrostatics and mechanics.
AI.conclusion: Establishes NS and ESBS as distinct dynamic operating conditions and provides a practical framework for advancing interferometric PFM toward truly quantitative electromechanical metrology.

title: Synchronization, Kinematic Waves and Spike-Phase-Separation in Feedback Ising Neural Networks on Heterogeneous Graphs
summary: Structural heterogeneity constrains collective dynamics in complex systems. However, its analytical tractability out of equilibrium remains limited. In this work, we study a class of kinetic Ising neural networks driven out of equilibrium by a homeostatic feedback loop between the neuronal excitability and the population firing rate. Using a Curie-Weiss heterogeneous mean-field approximation validated by Monte Carlo simulations, we provide an analytical characterization of how a macroscopic synchronized limit cycle emerges via an Andronov-Hopf bifurcation on heterogeneous networks. We derive closed-form phase boundaries and show that the onset of oscillations is explicitly controlled by network heterogeneity through the degree moment ratio. Degree heterogeneity decouples the spiking rate per neuron m from the spiking rate per synapse u, generating physical phenomena absent in homogeneous systems. These include (i) kinematic waves of sequential, degree-ordered activations propagating from the network periphery to the hubs, and (ii) a low-temperature phase-separated state emerging via a pitchfork bifurcation. We prove that for highly heterogeneous topologies, this phase-separated fixed point stabilizes and dynamically destroys the synchronized limit cycle. These results provide a mathematical framework for understanding how heterogeneity regulates macroscopic oscillations and out-of-equilibrium transitions in neural networks

AI.tldr: This paper analytically characterizes how network structural heterogeneity controls collective dynamics in out-of-equilibrium kinetic Ising neural networks with homeostatic feedback. Using a Curie-Weiss heterogeneous mean-field approach validated by Monte Carlo simulations, the authors derive closed-form phase boundaries and show that degree heterogeneity (via the degree moment ratio) triggers a synchronized limit cycle through Andronov-Hopf bifurcation, produces kinematic waves of degree-ordered neural activation, and can stabilize a phase-separated state that destroys oscillations.
AI.motivation: Structural heterogeneity is known to constrain collective dynamics in complex systems, yet its analytical tractability far from equilibrium has remained limited. This work aims to fill this gap by providing a rigorous mathematical framework for how heterogeneity governs macroscopic oscillations and out-of-equilibrium transitions in neural networks.
AI.method: The authors study kinetic Ising neural networks driven out of equilibrium by a homeostatic feedback loop coupling neuronal excitability to the population firing rate. They employ a Curie-Weiss heterogeneous mean-field approximation, validated against Monte Carlo simulations, to obtain closed-form phase boundaries and analytically characterize bifurcations (Andronov-Hopf and pitchfork) on heterogeneous network topologies.
AI.result: The onset of oscillations is explicitly controlled by network heterogeneity via the degree moment ratio. Heterogeneity decouples the spiking rate per neuron (m) from that per synapse (u), producing kinematic waves of sequential, degree-ordered activations propagating from periphery to hubs, and a low-temperature phase-separated state via a pitchfork bifurcation. In highly heterogeneous topologies, the phase-separated fixed point stabilizes and dynamically destroys the synchronized limit cycle.
AI.conclusion: The study provides a mathematical framework demonstrating that network heterogeneity is a key regulator of macroscopic oscillations and out-of-equilibrium transitions, with heterogeneous topologies enabling physical phenomena absent in homogeneous systems.

title: An iterative method bridging DFT, disorder averaging, and experiment in intercalated materials: application to Au-intercalated graphene
summary: Intercalation can strongly modify the electronic dispersion of a host material, as directly revealed by angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES). We develop a general iterative method combining density functional theory (DFT), tight-binding (TB), disorder averaging within the self-consistent T-matrix approximation (SCTMA), and experiment, to construct an effective model of the intercalated system. DFT identifies the relevant microscopic degrees of freedom and constrains selected model parameters, while comparison of SCTMA calculations with experiment guides their further refinement. We apply this method to graphene intercalated with Au clusters and show that it reproduces the main ARPES signatures of the Au-cluster phase, including the broadening of the V12an Hove singularity and the emergence of kink-like features in the dispersion. The essential microscopic ingredients identified by the analysis are the hybridization between selected intercalant orbitals and the graphene states, together with an intercalation-induced local scattering potential.

AI.tldr: The authors develop a general iterative method combining DFT, tight-binding modeling, self-consistent T-matrix approximation (SCTMA), and ARPES experiments to construct effective models of intercalated systems, applying it to Au-intercalated graphene and successfully reproducing key ARPES signatures including van Hove singularity broadening and kink-like dispersion features.
AI.motivation: Intercalation strongly modifies the electronic dispersion of host materials as seen by ARPES, but constructing accurate effective models that capture these modifications requires a systematic approach bridging first-principles theory and experiment.
AI.method: An iterative framework is developed that integrates density functional theory (DFT) to identify relevant microscopic degrees of freedom and constrain model parameters, tight-binding (TB) modeling for the effective Hamiltonian, self-consistent T-matrix approximation (SCTMA) for disorder averaging, and ARPES comparison to refine parameters iteratively.
AI.result: Applying the method to graphene intercalated with Au clusters, the model reproduces the main ARPES signatures of the Au-cluster phase, including broadening of the van Hove singularity and emergence of kink-like features in the dispersion. The key microscopic ingredients identified are hybridization between specific intercalant orbitals and graphene states, plus a local intercalation-induced scattering potential.
AI.conclusion: The combined DFT-TB-SCTMA-experiment method provides a general and effective strategy for constructing quantitatively accurate models of intercalated systems, with Au-intercalated graphene serving as a successful demonstration case.

title: Thermal spin transport in easy-planar $d$-wave altermagnets controlled by magnetic field
summary: Altermagnets constitute a novel class of collinear spin-compensated materials in which magnon branches are spin-split even in the non-relativistic limit. The latter is the result of a more complex symmetry operation (compared to conventional antiferromagnets) that connects the two sublattices. Altermagnetic splitting strongly affects the magnon transport properties, leading, in particular, to the thermal magnon splitter effect in easy-axial $d$-wave altermagnets. Whether this effect also appears in easy-planar systems is not obvious, since the magnon branches do not carry a constant magnetic moment in this case. Here, we consider the easy-planar $d$-wave altermagnet of a rutile-type, e.g., NiF$_2$, and demonstrate the emergence of the altermagnetically generated magnon magnetic moment, which is momentum-dependent and possesses $d$-wave symmetry. This then leads to the spin-splitter effect, i.e., the emergence of a magnon-driven spin current (the flow of magnetic moment) in response to the applied temperature gradient. We also demonstrate that the corresponding thermal spin conductivity can be effectively tuned by an external magnetic field perpendicular to the easy plane.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that in easy-planar d-wave altermagnets of rutile type (e.g., NiF2), altermagnetic splitting generates a momentum-dependent magnon magnetic moment with d-wave symmetry, which leads to a spin-splitter effect—a magnon-driven spin current in response to a temperature gradient. The thermal spin conductivity can be tuned by an external magnetic field perpendicular to the easy plane.
AI.motivation: The thermal magnon splitter effect has been established in easy-axial d-wave altermagnets, but whether it occurs in easy-planar systems is unclear because magnon branches do not carry a constant magnetic moment in that case. The authors aim to resolve this question.
AI.method: The authors theoretically analyze the easy-planar d-wave altermagnet of rutile-type (e.g., NiF2), deriving the magnon magnetic moment generated by altermagnetic splitting and computing the resulting thermal spin conductivity and its response to an external magnetic field.
AI.result: The authors demonstrate the emergence of an altermagnetically generated magnon magnetic moment that is momentum-dependent with d-wave symmetry, leading to the spin-splitter effect—a magnon-driven spin current under a temperature gradient. The thermal spin conductivity can be effectively tuned by an external magnetic field perpendicular to the easy plane.
AI.conclusion: Easy-planar d-wave altermagnets exhibit the spin-splitter effect despite the non-constant magnetic moment of magnon branches, and the associated thermal spin conductivity is magnetically tunable via a perpendicular external field.

title: Topology of Shape and Data in Material Microstructures
summary: One of the challenges in microstructure analysis is the rigorous quantification of the shape, size, and spatial arrangement of the microstructure beyond comparison of average values. We expound on formal principles combining Topological Data Analysis (TDA) and non-Euclidean distances between curves to motivate novel perspectives on the form and nature of pattern and shape in images. Specifically, TDA descriptors extracting persistent topological structures are combined with product submanifold learning of separable shape tensors (SST) to offer unique insights about electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) images of material microstructures through the lens of a dual-parameter filtration. Beyond standard approaches, our methodology highlights how different choices or permutations of shape distances can lead to distinct notions of topological persistence, thereby broadening the interpretive scope of TDA. The resulting visualizations of feature extraction are designed to be both principled and explanatory, offering novel tools for modern imaging science with applications to material metrology. More broadly, this framework has strong potential to impact domains where precise quantification of topology and shape is critical for uncovering fundamental image patterns and features, and enables additional data-driven tools for microstructure analysis.

AI.tldr: This paper combines Topological Data Analysis (TDA) with non-Euclidean distances between curves and product submanifold learning of separable shape tensors (SST) to rigorously quantify shape, size, and spatial arrangement in material microstructure images, specifically electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) images. Using a dual-parameter filtration, the framework reveals how different shape distance choices affect topological persistence and provides novel visualizations for microstructure analysis with broad implications for material metrology and imaging science.
AI.motivation: Traditional microstructure analysis relies on comparing average values, which fails to rigorously quantify the shape, size, and spatial arrangement of microstructural features. There is a need for formal, principled approaches that go beyond averaged metrics to capture the full complexity of pattern and shape in images.
AI.method: The methodology combines TDA descriptors that extract persistent topological structures with product submanifold learning of separable shape tensors (SST). The framework employs a dual-parameter filtration on EBSD images and explores different choices/permutations of non-Euclidean shape distances between curves, each yielding distinct notions of topological persistence.
AI.result: The approach demonstrates how different shape distance choices and permutations lead to distinct topological persistence interpretations, broadening the interpretive scope of TDA. The resulting feature extraction visualizations are principled and explanatory, providing novel tools for material metrology and modern imaging science.
AI.conclusion: The framework offers novel perspectives on pattern and shape quantification in microstructure analysis, with strong potential to impact domains requiring precise topology and shape quantification. It enables additional data-driven tools for microstructure analysis and broader imaging science applications.

title: Convergence to the exact kinetics of the one-dimensional Riviera model
summary: The Riviera model is a random sequential deposition model for house building on a lattice, in which a house cannot be built when both nearest-neighbor sites are already occupied. In one dimension, an attempted deposition is therefore rejected whenever the target site is an isolated vacancy. Despite the apparent simplicity of this rule, no exact analytical solution of the original model is currently known. We derive an infinite hierarchy of kinetic equations governing its dynamics and introduce a systematic closure scheme that can be implemented at arbitrary finite order. Solving the resulting systems order by order, we show that the corresponding kinetics converges rapidly toward the exact behavior. At high order, the method yields an exceptionally accurate estimate of the jamming density while retaining explicit analytical expressions for the full time-dependent evolution.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a systematic closure scheme for an infinite hierarchy of kinetic equations describing the Riviera model of random sequential deposition in one dimension, where deposition is rejected at isolated vacancies. Solving order by order, the kinetics converges rapidly to exact behavior, yielding exceptionally accurate jamming density estimates and explicit analytical time-dependent solutions.
AI.motivation: The Riviera model, a deceptively simple random sequential deposition process where a house cannot be built when both nearest-neighbor sites are occupied, has no known exact analytical solution despite its apparent simplicity. The authors aim to address this gap by developing a tractable analytical framework.
AI.method: The authors derive an infinite hierarchy of kinetic equations governing the model's dynamics and introduce a systematic closure scheme implementable at arbitrary finite order. The resulting systems are solved order by order to approximate exact behavior.
AI.result: The kinetics converges rapidly toward exact behavior with increasing closure order. At high order, the method provides an exceptionally accurate estimate of the jamming density while retaining explicit analytical expressions for the full time-dependent evolution.
AI.conclusion: The proposed hierarchy-closure approach offers a powerful and accurate analytical tool for the Riviera model, overcoming the lack of an exact solution and providing high-precision estimates of key quantities such as the jamming density.

title: Effects of gold cluster intercalation in graphene: stationary waves and modified QPI features
summary: Gold intercalation beneath epitaxial graphene on SiC produces a cluster phase with unusual standing waves and quasiparticle-interference (QPI) features concentrated near the graphene M points. We show that this can be explained by Au intercalation below graphene hollow sites, which induces a local scattering potential on the six surrounding carbon atoms. Within a T-matrix treatment, this ring-like scatterer produces elliptical QPI structures centered near M, in agreement with the experimental FT-STS measurements. We further show that these QPI features naturally generate the nearly stationary standing-wave patterns observed in real space. Finally, we compute the local-density-of-states contrast on and off a small cluster and show that its sign and magnitude are strongly energy dependent, consistent with the experimental observations.

AI.tldr: The paper explains that Au intercalation beneath epitaxial graphene on SiC creates a cluster phase showing unusual standing waves and quasiparticle-interference (QPI) features near the graphene M points. Using a T-matrix treatment with a ring-like scatterer model, the authors reproduce the elliptical QPI structures, the nearly stationary standing-wave patterns, and the energy-dependent local-density-of-states contrast observed in FT-STS experiments.
AI.motivation: To explain the origin of the unusual standing waves and quasiparticle-interference features near the graphene M points observed in experiments on Au-intercalated epitaxial graphene on SiC.
AI.method: The authors model Au atoms intercalated below graphene hollow sites as inducing a local scattering potential on the six surrounding carbon atoms. They use a T-matrix treatment to compute quasiparticle interference and local-density-of-states.
AI.result: The ring-like scatterer model produces elliptical QPI structures centered near the M points, matching experimental FT-STS data. The QPI features generate nearly stationary standing-wave patterns in real space, and the calculated LDOS contrast on and off a small cluster is strongly energy dependent, consistent with experiments.
AI.conclusion: Au intercalation below graphene hollow sites creates a ring-like local scattering potential on surrounding carbon atoms, which fully explains the anomalous QPI and standing-wave phenomena observed in epitaxial graphene on SiC.

title: Coupled Spin-Density-Wave and Bond-Order Driven Metal-Insulator Transition in Altermagnetic CsCr$_2$S$_2$O
summary: A metal-insulator transition (MIT) driven by bond order (BO) coupled with a secondary spin-density wave (SDW) is identified in CsCr$_2$S$_2$O. Such coupling is enabled as a result of the broken time-reversal symmetry due to the pre-existing C-type antiferromagnetic (C-AFM) order. First-principles calculations reveal an orbital-selective physics that Cr-$d_{yz}$ orbitals form local moments and establish the altermagnetic order, while the Cr-$d_{xz}$ orbitals remain metallic and hybridize with S-$p_z$. Thus the low-energy physics is governed by the Cr-$d_{xz}$ and S-$p_z$ orbitals. On-site interactions then enhance a secondary SDW ($s$SDW) instability of the itinerant $d_{xz}$ electrons, which couples to the Cr-$d_{xz}$-S-$p_z$ bonding order. The resulting coupled $s$SDW-BO simultaneously produces experimentally observed structural distortion, charge disproportionation, local Cr-moment modulation, and gap opening. Our results establish an orbital-selective mechanism upon which pre-existing altermagnetism and electronic correlations cooperate to drive a structural MIT.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies a metal-insulator transition in CsCr2S2O driven by bond order coupled with a secondary spin-density wave, enabled by pre-existing altermagnetic order. Orbital-selective physics shows Cr-dyz orbitals form local moments and establish altermagnetism, while Cr-dxz orbitals remain metallic and hybridize with S-pz. On-site interactions enhance a secondary SDW instability that couples to Cr-dxz-S-pz bonding order, producing structural distortion, charge disproportionation, local moment modulation, and gap opening simultaneously.
AI.motivation: To understand how pre-existing magnetic order and electronic correlations cooperate to drive a structural metal-insulator transition, establishing a mechanism based on orbital selectivity.
AI.method: First-principles calculations revealing orbital-selective physics in CsCr2S2O, showing that Cr-dyz orbitals form local moments and establish altermagnetic order while Cr-dxz orbitals remain metallic and hybridize with S-pz. Analysis of on-site interactions enhancing a secondary spin-density wave instability coupled to bonding order.
AI.result: A coupled secondary SDW-bond order simultaneously produces experimentally observed structural distortion, charge disproportionation, local Cr-moment modulation, and gap opening, identifying a MIT driven by bond order with a secondary SDW in CsCr2S2O.
AI.conclusion: An orbital-selective mechanism is established wherein pre-existing altermagnetism and electronic correlations cooperate to drive a structural metal-insulator transition.

title: Temperature-doping phase diagram and endurance in Ce-doped HfO2
summary: The structural and ferroelectric properties of epitaxial Hf1-xCexO2 (CHO) thin films in the ultrathin regime are investigated as a function of Ce concentration (5% <= x <= 20%) and temperature. A temperature-doping phase diagram is established for 10 nm films, showing a systematic evolution from the ferroelectric orthorhombic phase to tetragonal and cubic phases with increasing Ce content. The orthorhombic-tetragonal transition temperature decreases from ~800°C at x = 5% to $~300°C$ at x = 15%, indicating strong stabilization of higher-symmetry phases with doping. Consistently, the remanent polarization decreases from ~15 to $3.8 μC/cm2$ as x increases from 5% to 20%. In contrast, the endurance improves significantly, with higher Ce concentrations exhibiting markedly enhanced cycling stability up to 108 cycles. The opposing trends of polarization and endurance are correlated with reduced orthorhombic distortion, suggesting that fatigue mitigation in Ce-doped HfO2 is linked to structural evolution. These results provide a framework for optimizing composition and reliability in ultrathin ferroelectric HfO2 devices.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates epitaxial Hf1-xCexO2 (CHO) ultrathin films across Ce concentrations (5-20%) and temperatures, establishing a temperature-doping phase diagram that reveals a transition from ferroelectric orthorhombic to tetragonal/cubic phases with increasing Ce. Remanent polarization drops from ~15 to ~3.8 μC/cm², while cycling endurance improves to 10⁸ cycles, correlating with reduced orthorhombic distortion.
AI.motivation: To understand and optimize the trade-off between ferroelectric polarization and endurance in ultrathin Ce-doped HfO2 films by establishing the structural-phase behavior as a function of doping concentration and temperature.
AI.method: Epitaxial Hf1-xCexO2 thin films (10 nm) were grown and systematically characterized via structural and ferroelectric measurements across Ce concentrations (5% ≤ x ≤ 20%) and temperatures. A temperature-doping phase diagram was constructed, and polarization, endurance cycling (up to 10⁸ cycles), and phase transition temperatures were tracked as functions of Ce content.
AI.result: The orthorhombic-tetragonal transition temperature decreases from ~800°C at 5% Ce to ~300°C at 15% Ce. Remanent polarization drops from ~15 to 3.8 μC/cm² as Ce increases from 5% to 20%, while endurance improves markedly up to 10⁸ cycles. These opposing trends correlate with reduced orthorhombic distortion with doping.
AI.conclusion: Ce doping stabilizes higher-symmetry phases in ultrathin HfO2, reducing polarization but significantly enhancing cycling endurance. The findings provide a framework for optimizing composition-reliability trade-offs in ultrathin ferroelectric HfO2 devices.

title: Current-based RF charge sensing in a carbon nanotube
summary: Ultra-sensitive charge detection is a widely used tool for quantum electronics with applications in quantum information processing and in probing the physics of condensed matter systems. Existing approaches require either an impedance-matched resonant circuit, or millimeter-scale proximity between amplifier and sample, both adding complexity and constraining device design. In this work, we introduce a current-mode charge sensor in a suspended carbon nanotube, operating at the $1.25$ MHz resonance of an RLC tank circuit and achieving a charge sensitivity of $0.15~μe/\sqrt{\mathrm{Hz}}$. We utilize it to measure a double quantum dot (DQD) electrostatically defined in the same nanotube, revealing a highly regular charge stability diagram. We perform single-shot readout of the DQD charge state at an integration time of $3.56~μ\mathrm{s}$, without any false assignments over $10^{7}$ measurements and a signal-to-noise ratio of 17 exceeding the state of the art.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a novel current-mode charge sensor based on a suspended carbon nanotube operating at 1.25 MHz RLC resonance, achieving 0.15 μe/√Hz charge sensitivity. The sensor is used to measure an electrostatically defined double quantum dot in the same nanotube, enabling single-shot readout at 3.56 μs integration time with SNR of 17 and zero false assignments over 10^7 measurements, exceeding state of the art.
AI.motivation: Existing ultra-sensitive charge detection methods require either impedance-matched resonant circuits or millimeter-scale amplifier-sample proximity, both of which add complexity and constrain device design. The authors aim to overcome these limitations with a simpler approach.
AI.method: The authors introduce a current-mode charge sensor implemented in a suspended carbon nanotube. The sensor operates at the 1.25 MHz resonance of an RLC tank circuit and is used to measure a double quantum dot electrostatically defined in the same nanotube via single-shot readout.
AI.result: The sensor achieves a charge sensitivity of 0.15 μe/√Hz. It reveals a highly regular charge stability diagram of the DQD and performs single-shot readout at 3.56 μs integration time with no false assignments over 10^7 measurements and a signal-to-noise ratio of 17, exceeding the state of the art.
AI.conclusion: The current-mode charge sensor in a suspended carbon nanotube provides a simplified and ultra-sensitive charge detection approach that avoids the complexity of impedance-matched circuits and proximal amplifiers, achieving state-of-the-art performance in single-shot DQD charge readout.

title: Field-Selected Topological Buffering in a Disordered Skyrmion Crystal
summary: Quenched disorder can disrupt crystalline order without immediately destroying the topology of its constituent textures, but the relation between these processes in skyrmion crystals remains unclear. Using large-scale simulations of a triangular-lattice chiral magnet with random DM interactions, we show that the magnetic field selects between two disordering routes. At high fields, global translational coherence is lost at a weak-disorder scale, while sixfold bond-orientational order survives to a larger disorder strength and the total topological charge remains nearly locked up to a substantially larger scale. The resulting interval defines a topological buffer containing a Bragg-glass- like skyrmion regime followed by a skyrmion-glass regime. Finite-size scaling, spatial correlations, defect statistics, and spin autocorrelations support their distinct structural and glassy character. At lower fields, bond-orientational disordering nearly coincides with topological reconstruction, eliminating the skyrmion-glass window and contracting the buffer. These results identify the magnetic field as a control knob for separating crystalline disordering from topological-charge loss and establish topological buffering as a mechanism by which topological textures can remain robust in structurally disordered media.

AI.tldr: Using large-scale simulations of a triangular-lattice chiral magnet with random DM interactions, this paper shows that the magnetic field selects between two disordering routes in skyrmion crystals: at high fields, a topological buffer exists containing a Bragg-glass-like skyrmion regime followed by a skyrmion-glass regime, while at lower fields bond-orientational disordering nearly coincides with topological reconstruction, eliminating the skyrmion-glass window.
AI.motivation: To understand how quenched disorder disrupts crystalline order in skyrmion crystals without necessarily destroying the topology of their constituent textures, and to clarify the relation between crystalline disordering and topological-charge loss.
AI.method: Large-scale simulations of a triangular-lattice chiral magnet with random Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya (DM) interactions, employing finite-size scaling, spatial correlations, defect statistics, and spin autocorrelations to characterize the distinct structural and glassy phases.
AI.result: At high fields, translational coherence is lost at a weak-disorder scale, while bond-orientational order survives to larger disorder and topological charge remains locked up to a substantially larger scale, creating a topological buffer with a Bragg-glass-like skyrmion regime followed by a skyrmion-glass regime. At lower fields, bond-orientational disordering nearly coincides with topological reconstruction, contracting or eliminating the buffer.
AI.conclusion: The magnetic field acts as a control knob for separating crystalline disordering from topological-charge loss, and topological buffering is established as a mechanism by which topological textures can remain robust in structurally disordered media.

title: Beyond Hexagonal Boron Nitride: First-Principles Study of Pentaoctite-BN and Pop-BN Monolayers
summary: We investigate two novel non-hexagonal boron nitride monolayers, pentaoctite-BN (PO-BN) and pop-BN (PP-BN), using first-principles calculations. Their structural, electronic, mechanical, vibrational, thermal, and optical properties are systematically analyzed to assess their stability and potential applications. Despite being metastable with respect to hexagonal BN, both polymorphs satisfy the criteria for dynamical, mechanical, and thermal stability, indicating that they are viable two-dimensional materials. Both systems are indirect-gap semiconductors whose electronic states near the band edges are dominated by out-of-plane pz orbitals. Their distinct pentagon-octagon ring networks also give rise to different in-plane elastic anisotropies. Many-body optical calculations reveal strong excitonic effects and pronounced polarization-dependent optical absorption, with lattice engineering shifting the optical response from the ultraviolet toward the visible and infrared regions. These findings demonstrate that engineering non-hexagonal lattice architectures provides an effective strategy for tuning the electronic and optical properties of two-dimensional BN, highlighting PO-BN and PP-BN as promising candidates for future optoelectronic and photonic applications.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates two novel non-hexagonal boron nitride monolayers (pentaoctite-BN and pop-BN) via first-principles calculations, finding both are dynamically, mechanically, and thermally stable metastable indirect-gap semiconductors with strong excitonic effects and polarization-dependent optical absorption that can be tuned from UV to visible/infrared regions via lattice engineering.
AI.motivation: To explore whether engineering non-hexagonal lattice architectures in two-dimensional boron nitride provides an effective strategy for tuning electronic and optical properties, moving beyond the well-studied hexagonal BN structure.
AI.method: First-principles calculations systematically analyzing structural, electronic, mechanical, vibrational, thermal, and optical properties of two novel BN polymorphs (PO-BN and PP-BN), including many-body optical calculations to capture excitonic effects.
AI.result: Both polymorphs are metastable yet dynamically, mechanically, and thermally stable; they are indirect-gap semiconductors with pz-dominated band-edge states; they exhibit distinct in-plane elastic anisotropies due to different pentagon-octagon ring networks; strong excitonic effects and polarization-dependent absorption are observed, with lattice engineering shifting response from UV to visible/IR.
AI.conclusion: Non-hexagonal lattice engineering is an effective strategy for tuning 2D BN properties, and PO-BN and PP-BN are promising candidates for optoelectronic and photonic applications.

title: From Exact Diagonalization to DMRG: A Complete Numerical Study of the Transverse-Field Ising Model
summary: We present a self-contained numerical study of the one-dimensional transverse-field Ising model (TFIM), tracing its ground-state entanglement structure from exact diagonalization at small system size (L=8,14,20) through density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) calculations up to L=100. A single, consistent methodology - identical field grid, identical convergence diagnostic (independent runs at bond dimensions chi=100 and chi=200 at every point) - is used across all seven system sizes, and we show explicitly where exact diagonalization and DMRG must agree exactly rather than merely approximately. Along the way we document and resolve a bond-dimension convergence artifact that produced a spurious discontinuity in an earlier, less systematic dataset, as a worked cautionary example for practitioners. Using the resolved dataset we extract the central charge of the transition via two complementary routes - the leading logarithmic finite-size scaling of the mid-chain entropy, and the full Calabrese-Cardy formula applied to every bond of every system size simultaneously - obtaining c_eff to 0.51-0.52 as short-distance lattice corrections are systematically excluded, consistent with the exact two-dimensional Ising value c=1/2. We review the quantum-classical (Suzuki-Trotter) correspondence that underlies this agreement and discuss how the Widom-Kadanoff scaling hypothesis transplants from the classical to the quantum problem. The manuscript is intended as both a physics result and a worked methodological example of careful finite-size numerics.

AI.tldr: A systematic numerical study of the 1D transverse-field Ising model using exact diagonalization (L=8-20) and DMRG (up to L=100) with a consistent methodology, resolving a bond-dimension convergence artifact and extracting the central charge c=1/2 via two complementary routes.
AI.motivation: To provide a careful, self-contained numerical study of the TFIM ground-state entanglement structure with a single consistent methodology across system sizes, while documenting and resolving a convergence artifact that plagued an earlier dataset—serving as a worked cautionary example for practitioners.
AI.method: Uses exact diagonalization (L=8,14,20) and DMRG (up to L=100) with identical field grids and a convergence diagnostic of independent runs at bond dimensions chi=100 and chi=200. Central charge is extracted via (1) leading logarithmic finite-size scaling of mid-chain entropy and (2) full Calabrese-Cardy formula applied globally across all bonds and system sizes, while systematically excluding short-distance lattice corrections. The Suzuki-Trotter quantum-classical correspondence and Widom-Kadanoff scaling hypothesis are reviewed.
AI.result: Achieves c_eff = 0.51-0.52 after excluding short-distance lattice corrections, consistent with the exact 2D Ising value c=1/2. Demonstrates exactly where ED and DMRG must agree exactly, and resolves a spurious discontinuity from a bond-dimension convergence artifact in earlier data.
AI.conclusion: The study delivers both a physics result (confirming c=1/2 for the TFIM transition) and a methodological template for careful finite-size numerics, emphasizing systematic convergence diagnostics and the power of complementary central-charge extraction routes.

title: Anisotropic Tensile Strength and Fracture Mechanism of $θ$-TaN: A Machine-Learning Potential Molecular Dynamics Study
summary: theta-phase tantalum nitride (theta-TaN) combines metallic conductivity with exceptionally high thermal conductivity, making it a potential material for device thermal management and interconnect applications. However, its tensile strength and fracture behavior remain unclear. Here, we investigate the anisotropic tensile response and fracture mechanism of theta-TaN using neuroevolution-potential molecular dynamics simulations. Size-convergence tests show that a 20 nm long model is sufficient for reliable prediction, and the mechanical parameters vary by less than 3.5% over the strain-rate range of 10^7 to 10^9 s^-1. The results reveal strong tensile anisotropy. The c-axis direction ([0001]) shows a higher strength of 80.10 GPa and modulus of 748.63 GPa, but a lower fracture strain of 15.02%. In contrast, the a-axis direction ([2-1-10]) shows a lower strength of 56.87 GPa and modulus of 570.74 GPa, but a higher fracture strain of 17.71%. From 300 to 900 K, the mechanical properties decrease nearly linearly, while more than 73% of the 300 K strength is retained at 900 K. Fracture occurs without observable dislocation activity and is governed by cleavage-plane selection: {10-10} prismatic planes under a-axis tension and the (0001) basal plane under c-axis tension. Atomic displacement analysis shows that local separation and microvoid formation precede macroscopic crack growth, indicating a brittle fracture process driven by local bond-network instability. These results provide atomic-scale mechanical data for assessing the reliability of theta-TaN in thermal management applications.

AI.tldr: This paper uses neuroevolution-potential molecular dynamics simulations to investigate the anisotropic tensile response and fracture mechanism of θ-TaN, revealing strong tensile anisotropy (c-axis: 80.10 GPa strength, 748.63 GPa modulus; a-axis: 56.87 GPa strength, 570.74 GPa modulus), near-linear mechanical property degradation from 300–900 K, and brittle fracture governed by cleavage-plane selection without dislocation activity.
AI.motivation: θ-TaN is a promising material for device thermal management and interconnect applications due to its combination of metallic conductivity and exceptionally high thermal conductivity, but its tensile strength and fracture behavior remain unclear, limiting reliability assessment.
AI.method: Neuroevolution-potential molecular dynamics (NEP-MD) simulations were used to study the tensile response of θ-TaN. Size-convergence tests determined a 20 nm model length with <3.5% mechanical parameter variation over strain rates of 10^7–10^9 s^-1. Tensile loading was applied along the c-axis ([0001]) and a-axis ([2-1-10]) directions, with temperature effects examined from 300 to 900 K.
AI.result: Strong tensile anisotropy was found: c-axis loading gives higher strength (80.10 GPa) and modulus (748.63 GPa) but lower fracture strain (15.02%), while a-axis loading gives lower strength (56.87 GPa) and modulus (570.74 GPa) but higher fracture strain (17.71%). Mechanical properties decline nearly linearly from 300–900 K with over 73% of 300 K strength retained at 900 K. Fracture occurs without dislocation activity via cleavage-plane selection: {10-10} prismatic planes under a-axis tension and (0001) basal planes under c-axis tension. Atomic displacement analysis reveals local separation and microvoid formation preceding macroscopic crack growth, indicating brittle fracture from local bond-network instability.
AI.conclusion: The study provides atomic-scale mechanical data for θ-TaN including anisotropic strength, modulus, fracture strain, temperature dependence, and fracture mechanisms, enabling reliability assessment for thermal management and interconnect applications.

title: Lattice composite Fermi liquid with broken inversion symmetry
summary: We study transport in lattice composite Fermi liquids realized in half-filled Chern bands with broken inversion symmetry. We show that reduced crystalline symmetry exposes intrinsic singular dynamical responses of composite fermions that are otherwise hidden in the conventional Landau-level setting. At zero wave vector, inversion breaking allows gauge-field fluctuations to generate a non-analytic longitudinal optical resistivity, with $\operatorname{Re}ρ^{xx}(ω)\sim |ω|^{4/3}$ for gate-screened Coulomb interactions. At finite wave vector $\mathbf{q}$, inversion breaking leads to nonreciprocal transport and a non-analytic $\sim |\mathbf{q}|$ dependence of the Hall conductivity, both of which can be probed through surface acoustic wave propagation. We also discuss a distinct mechanism for singular DC transport in lattice composite Fermi liquids: renormalization of $2k_F$ scattering at the composite Fermi surface enhances Umklapp relaxation and can lead to a non-analytic temperature dependence of the resistivity. Taken together, our results identify transport signatures of lattice composite Fermi liquids that are absent in their continuum quantum Hall counterparts and can be directly tested in ongoing experiments on twisted MoTe$_2$ and rhombohedral graphene, where evidence for zero-field composite Fermi liquids has recently been reported.

AI.tldr: The paper studies transport in lattice composite Fermi liquids in half-filled Chern bands with broken inversion symmetry, revealing intrinsic singular dynamical responses—non-analytic longitudinal optical resistivity, nonreciprocal transport, and singular DC transport via renormalized 2kF scattering—that are absent in conventional Landau-level settings and can be probed experimentally.
AI.motivation: Composite Fermi liquids (CFLs) have traditionally been studied in the continuum Landau-level setting. The authors aim to understand how reduced crystalline symmetry (inversion breaking) in lattice settings exposes novel transport phenomena that are otherwise hidden, providing distinctive signatures of lattice CFLs distinct from their quantum Hall counterparts.
AI.method: The authors theoretically analyze transport in lattice CFLs in half-filled Chern bands with broken inversion symmetry. They examine gauge-field fluctuation effects at zero and finite wave vectors, analyzing the resulting optical resistivity, Hall conductivity, and DC transport. They also investigate a mechanism where renormalization of 2kF scattering at the composite Fermi surface enhances Umklapp relaxation.
AI.result: They find: (1) at zero wave vector, inversion breaking plus gauge-field fluctuations yield non-analytic longitudinal optical resistivity Reρxx(ω) ~ |ω|^{4/3} for gate-screened Coulomb interactions; (2) at finite wave vector q, inversion breaking causes nonreciprocal transport and non-analytic |q| dependence of Hall conductivity; (3) renormalized 2kF scattering enhances Umklapp relaxation, producing non-analytic temperature dependence of resistivity.
AI.conclusion: These results identify transport signatures unique to lattice composite Fermi liquids that are absent in continuum quantum Hall CFLs, and they can be directly tested in ongoing experiments on twisted MoTe2 and rhombohedral graphene where zero-field composite Fermi liquids have been reported.

title: Observation of long-lived spin order in nanoconfined water
summary: Liquids confined to nanometer-scale geometries exhibit behavior that departs markedly from their bulk counterparts, yet studying their dynamics under controlled conditions remains experimentally challenging. Here, we use nitrogen-vacancy (NV) center nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy to probe water confined in 5.6 nm channels as a function of temperature. The system remains liquid throughout the investigated temperature range and exhibits strongly suppressed diffusivity, enabling direct detection of its 1H NMR spectrum. Occasionally, the proton resonance transforms into a doublet with a splitting of several tens of kilohertz, which we tentatively attribute to hyperfine interactions mediated by long-lived paramagnetic charge complexes, in turn seeded by solvated electrons optically injected during laser illumination. The intermittent appearance of this feature suggests a metastable state comprising a correlated population of charge-hydration complexes extending throughout the confined liquid.

AI.tldr: Using NV-center NMR spectroscopy, the authors study water confined in 5.6 nm channels, finding it remains liquid with strongly suppressed diffusivity. They observe an intermittent proton resonance splitting into a doublet, tentatively attributed to hyperfine interactions from long-lived paramagnetic charge complexes seeded by solvated electrons, suggesting a metastable correlated charge-hydration state throughout the confined liquid.
AI.motivation: Confined water in nanoscale geometries behaves differently from bulk water, but studying its dynamics under controlled conditions is experimentally challenging. The authors aim to probe the NMR spectrum and dynamics of nanoconfined water to uncover these departures from bulk behavior.
AI.method: The study uses nitrogen-vacancy (NV) center NMR spectroscopy to measure 1H NMR spectra of water confined in 5.6 nm channels as a function of temperature. The confined system remains liquid and exhibits suppressed diffusivity, enabling direct spectral detection.
AI.result: The water remains liquid across the investigated temperature range with strongly suppressed diffusivity. The proton resonance occasionally transforms into a doublet with splitting of tens of kilohertz, attributed to hyperfine interactions mediated by long-lived paramagnetic charge complexes seeded by optically injected solvated electrons.
AI.conclusion: The intermittent doublet feature suggests the existence of a metastable state comprising a correlated population of charge-hydration complexes extending throughout the confined liquid, revealing novel behavior of nanoconfined water under illumination.

title: Physics to Circuit Analysis of GaN RF Integrated Circuits versus GaAs and Silicon
summary: The migration of radio-frequency (RF) integrated-circuit platforms from silicon to GaAs and now to gallium nitride is derived here from first principles. The hexagonal non-centrosymmetric GaN lattice admits a macroscopic polarization; elasticity and the piezoelectric tensor fix the bound sheet charge at an AlGaN/GaN interface, and Poisson's equation with triangular-well quantisation yields a degenerate quasi-two-dimensional channel of ~10^13 cm^-2 with no doping. Energy-momentum conservation for pair creation and phonon-limited energy relaxation set the breakdown field (3.3 MV/cm) and saturation velocity (2.5 x 10^7 cm/s), which combine into geometry-free limits V_brf_T = E_cv_sat/(2pi) and R_on^sp = 4V_br^2/(muepsilonE_c^3). These limits are mapped onto the low-noise amplifier, power amplifier, and switch/phase-shifter functions of a transmit/receive front end and quantified by a MATLAB device-physics model comparing GaN, GaAs, and Si up to 90 GHz. The purpose of this framework and its simulations is to identify which material platform offers the best performance at millimeter-wave frequency signals.

AI.tldr: This paper derives the fundamental physics limits of RF integrated-circuit material platforms (Si, GaAs, GaN) from first principles, and uses a MATLAB device-physics model to compare their performance up to 90 GHz for LNA, power amplifier, and switch/phase-shifter functions in a transmit/receive front end, concluding which platform best serves millimeter-wave applications.
AI.motivation: To identify which semiconductor material platform (Si, GaAs, or GaN) offers the best performance for RF integrated circuits at millimeter-wave frequencies, by deriving device limits from fundamental physics rather than empirical or ad-hoc comparisons.
AI.method: The authors derive physical limits from first principles: the GaN lattice's macroscopic polarization and piezoelectric effects determine bound sheet charge at the AlGaN/GaN interface; Poisson's equation with triangular-well quantization yields a ~10^13 cm^-2 2DEG with no doping. Energy-momentum conservation gives breakdown field (3.3 MV/cm) and saturation velocity (2.5 x 10^7 cm/s), from which geometry-free limits (V_br·f_T and R_on^sp) are derived. These are mapped onto LNA, PA, and switch/phase-shifter functions and quantified via a MATLAB device-physics model comparing Si, GaAs, and GaN up to 90 GHz.
AI.result: The framework and MATLAB simulations quantify and compare GaN, GaAs, and Si device performance across RF front-end functions up to 90 GHz, identifying the best material platform for millimeter-wave signals.
